70441.title: mon,osd: optionally preserve acting sets on pool crush_rule change
70441.author: FredNass
70441.body:
Changing an erasure-coded pool's CRUSH rule to a different failure domain today relocates far more data than the new rule requires: CRUSH recomputes placement statelessly, the balancer's pg_upmap_items are cancelled (`verify_upmap`) or pruned (source OSD gone from the new raw mapping), and nothing in that path looks at the acting set.

**Pool types.** The option works on both replicated and erasure-coded pools, but the benefit is essentially **erasure-coded**. `chooseleaf_indep` selects shards differently once the failure domain is raised, so a plain rule change reshuffles most shards and the balancer's upmaps go with them. `chooseleaf_firstn` (replicated, `chooseleaf_vary_r=1`) reuses the same seed and keeps each replica on its OSD unless two now share a failure-domain bucket, and most upmaps survive `check_pg_upmaps`. Evaluated offline on 8 production maps (30–1,600 OSDs), with a baseline that keeps upmaps passing `verify_upmap`: EC 6 pools / 5 clusters 81.1% → 26.7% of shards moved (3.04×, at the floor); replicated 94 pools / 5 clusters 8.1% → 8.0% (~1.0×, harmless). The replicated baseline was cross-checked against `osdmaptool` (per-PG mappings identical; a plain host→rack change moved exactly the floor).

Measured on a production map (1600 OSDs, EC 6+2, 16384 PGs, rack -> row): **84.5% of shards move while the failure-domain floor is 26.5%**; 78.6% of the pre-existing upmap entries are discarded outright. The balancer then re-moves part of the data again to fix the resulting imbalance.

The wipe is also *irreversible*: with `norebalance` set, changing the rule and immediately reverting it to its original value still leaves **12.15% of the shards (~3.45 PiB) misplaced on the same map, with zero bytes actually moved** — the revert restores raw CRUSH but not the cancelled upmap layer. With this feature enabled, that round trip becomes a true no-op (the revert re-pins to the unchanged, fully-compliant acting sets).

This PR adds an **opt-in, off-by-default** monitor behaviour: with `mon_crush_rule_change_preserve_acting` enabled, `ceph osd pool set <pool> crush_rule <rule>` stages, **in the same pending incremental as the rule change**,  pg_upmap_items that keep each shard on an OSD of its acting set whenever the new failure domain allows it, relocating only the genuine violators. OSDs see the rule and the pins atomically in one epoch — no `norebalance` dance, no transient full-pool misplacement window. Note that **no existing tooling covers this scenario**: CERN's `upmap-remapped.py` handles hardware add/remove and PG splits by pinning PGs back to their acting sets, but after a failure-domain change those acting sets violate the new rule, so the mons reject its pins (`verify_upmap`) and it has no mechanism to substitute compliant OSDs.

Results on the map above (movement identical to the theoretical floor, 26.6%, i.e. **3.2x less data moved**), depending on `mon_crush_rule_change_preserve_acting_fill_strategy`:

| fill strategy | data moved | per-OSD spread (CoV) | residual balancer work | pairs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `load-aware` (default) | 26.6% | **3.7%** | **1.4%** | ~55k |
| `hash` | 26.6% | 13.9% | 5.5% | ~42k |
| (today, plain rule change) | 84.5% | 15.6% | 6.2% | — |

Design points reviewers may want to weigh in on:

* **Safety guards** — pinning silently falls back to a plain rule change (with a `dout(1)` explanation) when `require_min_compat_client` <  luminous (same gate as the `osd pg-upmap-items` command), when a `pg_num` change is in flight (pins for merge sources would immediately be cleaned again), or when the pool exceeds  `mon_crush_rule_change_preserve_acting_max_pgs` (bounds the synchronous work in the command path; the load-aware scan is O(#osds in the rule  subtree) per relocated shard).

* **Consistency** — the pins are computed against a scratch map that applies everything already staged in the same paxos proposal (pending crush map, pending pools) plus the new rule, mirroring how `prepare_command

70458.title: rgw: add experimental cuObject S3 RDMA server support
70458.author: mkogan1
70458.body: Add experimental S3 RDMA server support using [NVIDIA cuObject](https://docs.nvidia.com/gpudirect-storage/cuobject/). S3 PUT and GET payloads transfer between client and RGW memory over RDMA, while authentication, headers, metadata and request status remain on HTTP. This integration is intended for testing and evaluation; configuration and behavior may change between releases. Key components: - `RGWCuObjServer` manages the server lifecycle, pre-registered buffer pool and per-thread channel IDs. - PUT reads client memory with RDMA_READ before passing the data through the existing checksum, compression and encryption filters. - GET collects the filtered response, including a selected range, and completes RDMA_WRITE before sending HTTP success. Ranged GETs report `206` in `x-amz-rdma-reply`. - RDMA bytes are included in Beast access logs and operations log accounting. Source and RPM builds include cuObject support by default (`WITH_RADOSGW_CUOBJ=ON`). The default ABI shim (`WITH_RADOSGW_CUOBJ_SHIM=ON`) loads `libcuobjserver.so.2` at runtime, configurable through `rgw_cuobj_library`. Building RGW requires no NVIDIA SDK or CUDA toolkit, and default dependency installation adds no NVIDIA repositories or packages. RDMA remains disabled at runtime until `rgw_cuobj_enabled=true` and `rgw_cuobj_rdma_ip` are configured; set `rgw_cuobj_rdma_port` as needed. With the shim, a missing library or required symbol leaves ordinary HTTP service available. GET and PUT requests carrying an RDMA token return HTTP 500 when cuObject is unavailable. For direct SDK linking, set `-DWITH_RADOSGW_CUOBJ_SHIM=OFF`, or use `--without cuobj_shim` for RPM builds. This requires `libcuobjserver-devel` at build time and the server runtime library when RGW starts, even with RDMA disabled. Install the SDK dependencies with: ```sh env WITH_RADOSGW_CUOBJ_SHIM=OFF ./install-deps.sh ``` Container RPM examples (use `-d rocky9` for EL9): ```sh # Default runtime shim ./src/script/build-with-container.py -d rocky10 -e source-rpm -e rpm # Direct linking; also installs the NVIDIA SDK in the build container ./src/script/build-with-container.py -d rocky10 --without-rgw-cuobj-shim -e source-rpm -e rpm ``` Automatic SDK installation supports Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, RHEL and CentOS Stream 9/10 on x86_64 and aarch64, using NVIDIA's matching RHEL repository. Fedora supports the default shim build; automatic direct-link setup reports an error because NVIDIA's Fedora repository lacks `libcuobjserver-devel`. To omit cuObject support, use `-DWITH_RADOSGW_CUOBJ=OFF` or `--rpmbuild-arg=--without=cuobj`. See the [S3 RDMA guide](https://github.com/mkogan1/ceph/blob/wip-rgw-s3rdma01/doc/radosgw/s3rdma.rst) and [container build instructions](https://github.com/mkogan1/ceph/blob/wip-rgw-s3rdma01/ContainerBuild.md) for runtime dependencies and configuration. Validation: cuObject unit suites pass in both modes without RDMA hardware. CMake/RPM options and container commands/cache checks pass; SDK installation was verified in Rocky 9 and 10 containers. Hardware testing requires the cuObject server 2.x runtime on RGW, a cuObject-aware client with its runtime dependencies, and an RDMA network with ConnectX-5 or newer NICs (ConnectX-4 is unsupported). To test with vstart, add the RDMA settings: ``` env MON=1 OSD=1 MDS=0 MGR=1 RGW=1 NFS=0 ../src/vstart.sh ... -o rgw_cuobj_enabled=true -o rgw_cuobj_rdma_ip=10.64.66.207 ``` Generate RDMA traffic with a cuObject-aware client, such as NooBaa's `s3perf.js`: ``` env CONFIG_JS_S3_RDMA_ENABLED=true CUFILE_ENV_PATH_JSON="/etc/cuobj.json" node ./src/tools/s3perf.js --endpoint http://10.64.66.207:8000 --access_key b2345678901234567890 --secret_key b234567890123456789012345678901234567890 --bucket bkt --put --size 4 --size_units KB --concur 1 --time 1 --rdma --local_ip 10.64.66.207 ``` Observe RDMA traffic with [ibtop](https://github.com/JannikSt/ibtop): ``` cargo install ibtop ibtop ```

70459.title: rgw: combine duplicate HTTP header values before signature verification
70459.author: kchheda3
70459.body:
When a client sends the same HTTP header name on more than one field-line, RFC 7230 and the SigV4 specification treat it as a single header whose value is the comma-joined list of the individual values, and the client signs that combined form. This is hit in practice by the AWS SDKs, which add a second `Content-Encoding: aws-chunked` line alongside a user-supplied encoding when a checksum is requested, putting two `Content-Encoding` field-lines on the wire.

RGW's beast frontend recorded each header line via `RGWEnv::set()`, which overwrote any previous value, so only the last occurrence survived in the request environment. During SigV4 verification the server reconstructed the canonical header from that single value, computed a different signature, and rejected the request with `403 SignatureDoesNotMatch`.

This change combines repeated header values in the order they arrive on the wire, so the canonical header the server reconstructs matches what the client signed.

An s3test is added that signs the combined `gzip,aws-chunked` value while transmitting two separate `Content-Encoding` field-lines, and verifies the PUT succeeds and that `aws-chunked` is stripped from the stored encoding.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/75304

70476.title: librbd: implement group image remove modes for snapshot dependencies
70476.author: pkalever
70476.body:
Removing an image from a group currently ignores user group snapshot
dependencies. As a result, user group snapshots can continue to
reference an image that is no longer a member of the group. The
associated .group image snapshots are also retained.

Add a force flag to group image removal:

* force=false
    Return -EBUSY if the image is referenced by one or more user
    group snapshots.

* force=true
    Remove the image without checking for user group snapshot
    dependencies. Existing user group snapshots and their .group image
    snapshots are preserved. This matches the previous behavior.

Implement the force flag in librbd rather than only in the CLI.
Exposing the flag through the API provides consistent behavior across
the C, C++, Python, and CLI interfaces, avoids duplicating dependency
handling in callers, and keeps the CLI as a thin wrapper over the
librbd implementation.

The CLI adds:

--force              keep dependent user group snapshots

The default is safer because it prevents removing an image that is
still referenced by user group snapshots. Existing API entry points
and internal callers that rely on the previous behavior continue to
force removal.

Also add unit, Python, CLI help, and workunit coverage for the default
and forced behaviors.

Enables cephadm to run inside a container without `--privileged`, using explicit capabilities and bind-mounts instead.

### Changes

- **`src/cephadm/Containerfile`** — builds from `quay.ceph.io/ceph-ci/ceph:main`; installs required tools (systemd, D-Bus, lvm2, smartmontools, chrony, firewalld, etc.); copies cephadm sources and sets `/usr/sbin/cephadm` as entrypoint. Compatible with both `docker build` and `podman build`.

- **`src/cephadm/container-run.sh`** — reference run script that:
  - Auto-detects Podman or Docker (Podman preferred)
  - Drops `--privileged`; uses 14 explicit `--cap-add` flags (each documented with its rationale)
  - Uses `--network host` (required for host NIC/route visibility), `--pid host` and `--cgroupns host` (required for systemd/cgroup interaction — marked for future removal once process-checking is refactored to use D-Bus), `--ipc host`
  - Mounts `/run/systemd`, D-Bus socket, `/sys`, `/dev`, `/proc`, `/run/udev`, ceph data/log/config dirs, systemd unit dir, sysctl.d, logrotate.d, cephadm lock dir, and the container engine socket (Podman or Docker)
  - `--security-opt label=disable` for SELinux/AppArmor compatibility with the bind-mounts

```sh
# bootstrap example
CEPHADM_IMAGE=quay.ceph.io/ceph-ci/ceph:main ./src/cephadm/container-run.sh bootstrap --mon-ip 192.168.1.10

# inspect block devices
./src/cephadm/container-run.sh ceph-volume lvm list
```

`--pid host` and `--cgroupns host` are intentionally included for now; they can be removed once cephadm's process inspection is refactored to use `systemctl`/D-Bus queries exclusively.

70506.title: common/admin_socket: unlink stale sockets left by a killed daemon on restart
70506.author: lumir-sliva
70506.body:
Unprivileged daemons (radosgw, rbd-mirror, ...) default their admin socket to a per-process path embedding $pid and $cctid ($cluster-$name.$pid.$cctid.asok) so multiple instances of the same daemon can coexist. That file is only unlinked on a graceful exit, through add_cleanup_file()/atexit().

A daemon killed with SIGKILL skips that cleanup and leaves its socket behind in the run dir. Both `ceph orch daemon restart --force` and container/pod restarts kill the process this way. Since the next instance picks a new $pid/$cctid, bind_and_listen()'s same-path stale-socket unlink never revisits the old file, so dead sockets pile up one per forced restart:

```
# ls /run/ceph/<fsid>/
...rgw...gjcmla.2.100116160633216.asok   <- dead, connection refused
...rgw...gjcmla.2.94007843477888.asok    <- current
```

Reported on cephadm and reproduced on Rook, so this is fixed daemon-side in common/ rather than in the orchestrator.

AdminSocket::init() now sweeps the run directory before binding and unlinks the daemon's own sibling sockets that no longer answer a ping. The daemon identity comes from the "$cluster-$name." (or "$name.") prefix, so:
- other daemons' sockets are never considered,
- a live concurrent instance answers the ping and is left untouched,
- only actual sockets are considered (is_socket guard).

Windows is guarded out (no behavior change there).

Validated on a vstart RGW: a forced restart no longer leaks the old socket, graceful shutdown still cleans its own, and both a live same-name instance and other entities' sockets are left alone. Added unit test AdminSocket.UnlinkStaleSiblingSockets covering all four cases.

Tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/76939

70532.title: ptl-tool: add audit-and-relabel option to --qe-label ticket prompt
70532.author: yuriw
70532.body:
## Summary

At the `--qe-label` interactive ticket-decision prompt (the one that fires when exactly one open QA ticket already matches the label: `Do you want to update this existing QA ticket? [y/n/o/q]`), adds a new **`a`** option: *audit tracker & relabel tested PRs*.

## Logic steps

1. Check the matched tracker's Redmine status. If it isn't exactly `QA Approved`, print the current status and re-prompt — nothing is touched until QA has actually signed off.
2. If approved, prompt for which label to relabel, defaulting to the `--qe-label` value already in hand (more reliable than the tracker's own "Ceph PR Label" custom field, which is blank on many tickets).
3. Fetch every **open** PR on the target repo carrying that label via the GitHub REST issues endpoint (paginated through the existing `get()` helper) and show the list.
4. Prompt for target labels to apply, defaulting to `TESTED` + `ready-to-merge`, editable to whatever's actually needed.
5. Show the full plan and require an explicit `[y/N]` confirmation (or, under `--dry-run`, print the plan and stop there) before mutating anything.
6. Apply via REST `POST` of the new labels per PR **first**, then REST `DELETE` of the old label (not `gh pr edit`/GraphQL, which needs OAuth scopes a repo-scoped token doesn't have). Adding first means a failed request never leaves a PR with neither label. Logs but doesn't abort on a per-PR failure, so one bad PR doesn't block the rest of the batch — but exits non-zero if literally every PR in the batch failed, since a "no-op that reports success" is worse than a crash.
7. On completion, print a message and exit — this is a terminal action for the current invocation; rerun `ptl-tool.py` to start a fresh round.

## Review round 2 (fixes since first review)

A second review caught 7 real issues, all fixed:
- **DELETE-then-POST could orphan a PR** (old label removed, new labels never added, if POST failed after a successful DELETE) — reordered to POST-first.
- **Empty target-labels input** (e.g. `,,,` — non-blank but parses to `[]`) was silently accepted as "remove old label, add nothing" — now rejected before the plan/confirm step.
- **A fully-failed batch still returned `'completed'`**, which the caller treats as unconditional success — now `sys.exit(1)` if nothing actually updated.
- **The DELETE URL interpolated the label raw** — now percent-encoded via `urllib.parse.quote`.
- **PR titles could contain non-ASCII characters and crash printing** under a non-UTF-8 stdout — the same bug class already fixed once for this function's own UI strings, except titles are external data we can't just rewrite as ASCII ourselves — now normalized defensively before printing.
- **The `state=open` query param and the `pull_request`-key filter were both unverified** — every existing test fixture hardcoded `pull_request:{}` on every item, so a mixed open/closed/merged response was never actually exercised. Added tests for both.

## Testing

- 28 new unit tests added to `src/script/test_ptl_tool.py` (all mock `session`/`input`, no live network needed): not-approved short-circuit, cancel at each prompt, no-open-PRs no-op, `--dry-run` never touching `session.delete`/`session.post`, custom label and custom target-labels input, empty-target-labels rejection, multi-PR apply, per-PR `POST`/`DELETE` failure handling in both orders (including the no-orphaning guarantee and the all-failed `sys.exit(1)` case), label URL percent-encoding, non-ASCII PR titles, the GitHub query explicitly requesting `state=open`, and a mixed-response case where a plain issue sharing the label with real PRs is correctly excluded. All 28 tests in the file (4 pre-existing + 24 new) pass — verified independently on both soko04 and vossi02.
- Live-verified against real trackers/PRs on `ceph/ceph` (via `--dry-run`, no mutation): the not-approved path (real tracker in `QA Testing` status, correctly loops back to the prompt), and the full happy path (real `QA Approved`

70535.title: rados: simple autoscaler with effective ratio
70535.author: mmgaggle
70535.body:
This RFC adds **simple autoscaling**: pools are provisioned by an absolute share of the PG-per-OSD budget, plans are always visible before they run, and whether the autoscaler may *act* stays exactly where it has always lived — in `pg_autoscale_mode`.

**History:** reworked 2026-07-25 per review (integer unit, warn-only overcommit, decrement confirmation, shadow-root scoping); revised 2026-07-27 to a budget fraction; redesigned 2026-07-28 into the mode x plan separation below, which deletes the new mode values entirely — `pg_autoscale_mode` keeps its classic `on|warn|off` vocabulary and meanings.

## Motivation

Operators who think in a per-OSD PG budget ("every OSD should carry 200-250 PG replicas") today either turn the autoscaler off and hand-compute `pg_num`, or reverse-engineer `target_size_ratio` weights that later pools silently renormalize and usage overrides. Beyond the arithmetic, the deeper operational complaint is *autonomy*: the autoscaler moves data when the cluster changes, at times of its choosing.

## Design

Two orthogonal axes:

* **`effective_ratio`** decides what the *plan* is: pg_num = ratio x budget / size, absolute (never renormalized, never overridden by usage). The **`simpleautoscale` cluster flag is the master switch** — ratios may be declared or pre-staged at any time but are inert until the flag is set; unsetting it is a complete rollback to legacy autoscaling.
* **`pg_autoscale_mode`** keeps deciding whether the autoscaler may act, with its classic values: `on` acts, `warn` warns, `off` opts out. The machinery never touches a pool's mode.

Each pool's **plan state is derived, never stored** (`osd pool get pg_autoscale_plan`, PLAN column): `learn` (no ratio yet), `pending` (plan differs from pg_num; stamped as `planned_pg_num`, listed by `POOL_AUTOSCALE_PENDING`), `current` (nothing to do).

**Acceptance is a mon command, atomic in one osdmap transaction** — apply exactly the stamped plans the operator reviewed, clear the stamps. This is why it is a command rather than a pool param: one pool, several, or `--all` are validated up front and committed together in a single osdmap epoch, so a reviewed plan-set (say, twenty pools after an expansion) applies as one change or not at all:

```
ceph osd pool autoscale-accept <pool> [<pool> ...] [--all] [--yes-i-really-mean-it]
```

Mode `warn` pools wait for it. Mode `on` pools invoke the same path automatically — with one exception: a plan that merges away more than half the PGs of a pool storing more than `mon_osd_pool_pg_merge_confirm_bytes` (default 1 TiB) is **held pending for manual confirmation**. Growth is hands-off; destructive shrinks get a human sign-off. That closes the merge-storm-on-OSD-loss hole even for fully autonomous pools.

For example — the cluster grows, a `warn` pool's plan diverges and waits:

```
$ ceph health detail
[WRN] POOL_AUTOSCALE_PENDING: 1 pools have autoscaler plans awaiting acceptance
    Pool bar plan pg_num 1024 awaits acceptance (current pg_num 512)
$ ceph osd pool autoscale-status
POOL  EFFECTIVE RATIO  PG_NUM  NEW PG_NUM  AUTOSCALE  PLAN
bar            0.4000     512        1024  warn       pending
$ ceph osd pool autoscale-accept bar
pool 'bar' accepted plan: pg_num 512 -> 1024
```

**Greenfield** — one line per pool, born at the right size, plan `current` from birth:

```
ceph osd pool set simpleautoscale
ceph config set global mon_target_pg_per_osd 250
ceph osd pool create foo erasure ec22 --effective-ratio 0.5
ceph osd pool create bar --effective-ratio 0.4
ceph osd pool create baz --effective-ratio 0.1
```

`--dry-run` previews the computed pg_num without creating; `pool get effective_ratio` returns the declared fraction verbatim. Plans are scoped to real budget domains (device-class shadow roots, overlap proration).

**Brownfield** — the runbook is no-op-by-construction:

```
ceph osd pool ls | while read p; do ceph osd pool set $p pg_autoscale_mode warn; done
ceph osd pool set simpleautoscale
```

Warn-first gua

70539.title: mgr/volumes: fix stale bytes_used in subvolume/subvolumegroup info
70539.author: LiShengG
70539.body:
`ceph fs subvolume info` and `ceph fs subvolumegroup info` intermittently report a stale `bytes_used`, including `0`, while `ceph.dir.rbytes` on the same directory is already non-zero.

## Root cause

`SubvolumeBase.info()` and `Group.info()` derive `bytes_used` from a directory `statx(CEPH_STATX_SIZE)`. `Client::statx_to_mask()` never sets `CEPH_STAT_RSTAT` for that mask, so the resulting getattr is not forced to the auth MDS: it can be answered by a replica MDS, or short-circuited from cached `Fs` caps without contacting the MDS at all. Either path can return a stale directory size (including the initial `0`) before fresh recursive usage is reflected.

Reading `ceph.dir.rbytes`, by contrast, goes through the vxattr getxattr path, which forces `CEPH_STAT_RSTAT` (`VXATTR_RSTAT`) and is routed to the auth MDS. This is why the two APIs, both meant to expose the same recursive byte count, can disagree at the same instant.

## Fix

Read `bytes_used` from the `ceph.dir.rbytes` vxattr instead, falling back to the statx size on `cephfs.NoData`. Besides fixing the staleness, `bytes_used` is a user-visible recursive-usage field, so querying the explicit rbytes interface is more correct than depending on the overloaded directory stat size, whose recursive meaning is conditional on `client_dirsize_rbytes`.

## Why not change `statx_to_mask()`

Changing `Client::statx_to_mask()` to request `CEPH_STAT_RSTAT` for every `CEPH_STATX_SIZE` statx would broaden behavior beyond the mgr/volumes info path and make ordinary directory size statx calls force rstat/auth-MDS handling. This fix keeps the scope local to the user-visible recursive usage field that explicitly needs rbytes semantics.

## Performance note

This changes each subvolume/subvolumegroup info call to issue one additional `ceph.dir.rbytes` vxattr lookup, which requests `CEPH_STAT_RSTAT` and may require an auth-MDS round trip instead of using cached statx data. The extra cost is limited to the info path and buys correctness for a field that is expected to report recursive usage. I can benchmark larger batch-listing scenarios if reviewers are concerned.

## Verification

vstart cluster, Ceph main (`21.3.0-1135-g0dfc8345236`), at `max_mds = 1`. This is the strongest control, since the answering MDS is necessarily the auth MDS. Paired sampling captures `bytes_used` and `ceph.dir.rbytes` on the same directory in the same iteration.

| | pre-fix (buggy) | post-fix |
|---|---|---|
| subvolume: `bytes_used = 0` while `ceph.dir.rbytes > 0` | hit within 50 iterations | **0 / 300** |
| subvolumegroup: same signature | hit at iteration 8 | **0 / 246** |

Across 546 paired samples the bug signature did not occur once. `bytes_used` now tracks `ceph.dir.rbytes` exactly, apart from sub-second sampling lag during active writes (inherent rstat propagation, both values non-zero). The pre-fix baseline reproduced the zero within 50 iterations under the identical setup.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/78671

70549.title: script/ptl-tool: check PR review approvals before merging a --pr-label batch
70549.author: yuriw
70549.body:
## What

Adds `check_pr_approvals()`, a pre-flight approval gate for `--pr-label`/`--integration`/`--qe-label` merges. It's the native `ptl-tool.py` equivalent of the standalone `ptl-check-approvals.sh` script, folded directly into the tool's own flow instead of requiring a separate manual pre-check.

## Where it runs

Right after the label search builds the `prs` list (`Will merge PRs: [...]`), and *before* the existing PRE-FLIGHT base-branch consistency check. This way, if a PR gets excluded here, it never even reaches the base-branch check.

## Behavior

Fetches every PR's `reviewDecision` via one batched GraphQL query (aliased `pr0`, `pr1`, ... — same computed field `gh pr list --json reviewDecision` reads; GitHub only exposes it over GraphQL, not REST). If none are `REVIEW_REQUIRED`, it's a silent no-op. If some are, it prints them and prompts:

```
How do you want to handle unapproved PRs? [a/r/i]
  a = accept and proceed, posting a reminder comment on each unapproved PR
  r = remove the label from unapproved PRs and exclude them from this run
  i = ignore and proceed with no changes
```

- `a`: PRs stay in the merge batch; each gets an `@author` reminder comment (same message the bash script's `--comment` posts).
- `r`: label removed from each unapproved PR via `DELETE .../labels/{label}` (404 treated as already-gone, not an error), and those PRs are dropped from this run's merge list. If every PR in the batch is unapproved, exits non-zero rather than merging nothing.
- `i`: proceeds exactly as before this feature existed — no comment, no label change.

`--ci-mode` skips the prompt entirely (logs a warning, proceeds with all PRs), matching the tool's existing non-interactive contract for `--ci-mode` elsewhere. `--dry-run` skips the comment/DELETE calls but the returned PR list still reflects what a real run would do, so a dry run's PRE-FLIGHT/merge preview matches reality.

## Testing

17 new unit tests (`src/script/test_ptl_tool.py`, mocked session/input, no live network) — no-op on all-approved, GraphQL query batching, GraphQL-error exit, ci-mode skip, accept/remove/ignore paths (including multi-PR accept), remove-all-unapproved exit, 404-on-delete handling, dry-run guards, invalid-input reprompt, non-ASCII title normalization, unresolvable-PR-node fail-closed, and unknown-author mention handling. 25/25 pass (8 pre-existing + 17 new).

Also live-validated end-to-end against real PRs (read-only GraphQL query directly, plus the full interactive flow via a real `--pr-label` batch under `--dry-run`) — correctly identified real unapproved PRs, handled the `a/r/i` prompt, and independently confirmed zero mutation occurred (label still present on GitHub after a dry-run `r` choice).

Signed-off-by: Yuri Weinstein <yweinste@redhat.com>

70555.title: client: don't conclude ENOENT locally in complete snapped directories
70555.author: xiubli
70555.body:
When a file is deleted after a snapshot was taken, the head dentry becomes null while a snap dentry (created by copy-on-write during unlink) preserves the file's inode for the snapshot.  Cache eviction can remove the snap dentry from cache, leaving only the null head dentry whose timestamp range inadvertently shadows all historical snapshot IDs.

On a subsequent snapshot lookup, the MDS finds this null dentry as a cache hit and incorrectly concludes the file does not exist — even though the real snap dentry is still on disk.  The client compounds this by skipping the MDS lookup entirely when its local directory cache is marked complete, which for snapshot views only guarantees head-dentry coverage, not snap-dentry coverage.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/78555
Reported-by: Andras Pataki <apataki@flatironinstitute.org>
Co-authored-by: Dhairya Parmar <dparmar@redhat.com>

70600.title: mon: reject device-class CRUSH rules for stretch mode
70600.author: tchaikov
70600.body:
A rule pinned to a device class takes from that class's shadow tree, so an OSD's dividing bucket resolves to "zone1~ssd" while degraded stretch mode records the surviving zone as the real "zone1". The two never match, so every PG of a pool on such a rule goes inactive once a zone is lost, and stays inactive, because the cluster leaves degraded stretch mode only once no PG is degraded, inactive or unknown.

No path into that state checked for it. `try_enable_stretch_mode()` looked at the bucket type, the subtree count and the weight skew, but never at the rule. `osd pool set <pool> crush_rule` only checked that the rule exists and matches the pool type. And a map injected with `osd setcrushmap` could add a class to a rule already in use. The cluster then reports healthy stretch mode right up until a zone is lost.

Refuse the rule in all three, the pool set unless `--yes-i-really-mean-it` is given. An injected map is refused only when it is what introduces the class, so a cluster already in this state can still change its crush map, not least to get itself out of it.

Spotting a class is cheap: `step take <root> class <class>` compiles into a take of that class's shadow bucket, so `get_rule_device_class()` can read the class back from any of a rule's take targets.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/78741

70627.title: osd: add bfq, a proportional-share op scheduler [RFC]
70627.author: mmgaggle
70627.body:
**RFC.** This series adds `bfq`, an experimental third OSD op scheduler
(`osd_op_queue = bfq`) modeled on the Linux BFQ elevator as exposed through
the cgroups v2 io controller. Marked draft to gather design feedback on the
integration points before further hardening; the algorithm core is
implemented, tested, and benchmarked below.

## Motivation

Two gaps in the current schedulers motivated this:

1. **No isolation between client workload types.** All client ops collapse
   into a single dmclock client under `mclock_scheduler`
   (`client_profile_id_t` is always default-constructed), so an RGW bulk
   ingest and latency-sensitive RBD traffic sharing OSDs contend FIFO within
   the client class; `wpq` round-robins per client session, so isolation
   dilutes as the busier workload opens more sessions. Neither has a dial
   for "protect block traffic from object traffic".

2. **Sensitivity to device capacity estimates.** mclock's reservation/limit
   tags are denominated in absolute IOPS, requiring the boot-time bench and
   `osd_mclock_max_capacity_iops_*`; a wrong estimate misdrives the
   scheduler (we reproduce this below on NVMe). BFQ is purely
   proportional-share: it distributes whatever throughput the OSD actually
   delivers according to weights and needs **no capacity estimate at all**.

## Design

Two-level B-WF2Q+ hierarchy over byte budgets; weights follow the cgroups v2
`io.bfq.weight` convention (1..1000, default 100, runtime-adjustable):

```
root
|-- client group                (osd_bfq_client_group_weight)
|   |-- block  (rbd pools)      |
|   |-- object (rgw pools)      | classified by pool
|   |-- file   (cephfs pools)   | application metadata
|   `-- other  (untagged)       |
`-- background group            (osd_bfq_background_group_weight)
    |-- recovery
    `-- best_effort              (scrub, snaptrim, pg delete)
```

Each backlogged leaf gets a byte budget (`osd_bfq_max_budget`, default 8 MiB
per the kernel) served exclusively until exhaustion/empty/timeout; finish
tags are computed over the assigned budget and back-shifted to consumed
service at expiration; the next budget adapts to observed demand. Client ops
map to streams via `pg_pool_t::application_metadata`, refreshed per epoch
through a new default-no-op `OpScheduler::update_from_osdmap()` hook called
from `OSDShard::consume_map()`. The `immediate` class and above-cutoff
priorities bypass through a strict queue exactly like mclock, as does
`enqueue_front`. `dequeue()` never returns a future time.

Deliberate scope exclusions (documented in the dev doc): no weight-raising
heuristics, no device idling/anticipation, service charged at dequeue
(dispatch) rather than completion — the same accounting model mclock uses.

Cross-cutting change reviewers should look at closely: the literal
`osd_op_queue == "mclock_scheduler"` comparisons gating byte-denominated
costs and recovery priority-class encodings (9 sites) are replaced by an
`op_queue_type_uses_qos_cost()` predicate, and the scrub-cost check inverts
to mclock-only so other schedulers never reach the `get_cost_per_io()`
abort. No behavior change for wpq or mclock.

## Evidence

**In-process microbenchmark** (`ceph_bench_op_scheduler`, included): identical
synthetic workloads through all three schedulers against a simulated 100 MB/s
device, mclock calibrated to the same rate. Backlogged rbd-pool victim vs
rgw-pool aggressor fanning out over client sessions:

| Aggressor sessions | wpq victim share | mclock victim share | bfq victim share |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 50.0% | 50.3% | 49.7% |
| 4 | 20.0% | 20.1% | 49.7% |
| 16 | 5.9% | 6.7% | **49.7%** |

Paced victim (20% of device) under an 8-session aggressor: bfq delivers the
offered rate at p99 83 ms (bounded by budget rotation); mclock delivers it at
p99 419 ms (FIFO behind the aggressor backlog); wpq caps the victim below its
offered rate entirely. Client-vs-recovery lands on each scheduler's own dial
(bfq 80/20 per group weights, mclock 50/50 pe

70638.title: msg/async: MSG_ZEROCOPY send path + PSP secure-mode scaffolding (RFC)
70638.author: mmgaggle
70638.body:
RFC: this series is the first, deliberately small slice of a messenger
zero-copy effort for the async (Posix) stack. It is posted as a draft to
get direction feedback before the larger pieces land. Everything here is
strictly default-off / no-op on the wire.

## AI assistance disclosure

Please read this series with that in mind. **All nine commits were
written with AI assistance** (Claude); each carries an `Assisted-by:`
trailer naming the model that worked on it. The design decisions,
problem selection, and the performance motivation are mine; the code,
comments, and commit messages were substantially AI-drafted and then
reviewed and corrected by me.

The series was also put through an AI-driven adversarial review before
this update, which found and fixed three real buffer-pin lifetime
defects (detailed below). I am flagging that not to suggest the code is
therefore safe, but because the opposite inference is the right one:
this is the area most deserving of careful human eyes, since a
zero-copy pin bug puts freed heap on the wire and the failure mode is
silent. The claims in this description that say "validated" or
"measured" were produced by actually running the jobs, not asserted.

## Motivation

On large-object send paths (RGW gets, EC full-stripe reads), every
payload byte the messenger sends passes through the kernel socket copy.
At NIC line rates this is a meaningful fraction of a node's DRAM
bandwidth, and it is pure overhead: the payload is already immutable,
refcounted memory by the time it reaches `cs.send()`. Linux
`MSG_ZEROCOPY` (4.14+) can elide that copy for large sends, provided the
buffer is kept alive (pinned) until the kernel posts a completion on the
socket error queue.

Secure mode is excluded from that win today: the per-frame AEAD in
`crypto_onwire` copies the payload during encryption, so there is no
copy left to elide. The last three commits scaffold a path out of that
box: PSP Security Protocol (kernel inline AEAD with NIC offload,
`linux/psp.h`, kernel v6.18+ on CX-7+/mlx5) as a new opt-in msgr2
connection mode (`secure-psp`), so that secure traffic can eventually be
both encrypted and zero-copy.

PSP Security is supported on ConnectX, and appears that we will see
support with Intel Mount Morgan and Broadcom Thor. The alternatives
to PSP Security for zero-copy for secure mode would be switching
messenger to kTLS, but that only covers the send side. Receive side
zero copy seems to only be possible with PSP Security. Thanks to
@bill-scales for pointing this out:

https://lwn.net/Articles/1082317/

## What's in the series

**Measurement first (commits 1–4)** — instrumentation and correctness
gates, so the copy volume is quantified before any behavior changes:

- Send-path copy-accounting perfcounters (`msgr_send_bytes_copied` /
  `_zerocopy`, an iovec-segments histogram, and
  `msgr_zerocopy_{submitted,completed,fallback,pinned_bytes}`).
- fio `ceph-msgr` engine: fragmented-payload mode (`payload_frags`) to
  reproduce RGW-multipart / EC scatter send shapes; EC R1/R2 read
  send-shape jobs; and a `verify_echo` data-integrity gate that
  round-trips the payload and self-checks crc32c+length (fio's native
  verify cannot gate this storageless pipe). The gate has an env-gated
  self-test (`CEPH_MSGR_VERIFY_ECHO_CORRUPT=1`) that demonstrates it
  catches a corrupted send without a rebuild.

**MSG_ZEROCOPY send (commits 5–6)** — `ms_tcp_zerocopy` (default false)
+ `ms_tcp_zerocopy_min_size` (default 16K). When enabled:
`SO_ZEROCOPY` opt-in at connect/accept, `MSG_ZEROCOPY` for data
segments above the threshold, per-send pinning of the refcounted
bufferlist until the `MSG_ERRQUEUE` completion retires it, drain on the
existing fd from `_try_send`, transparent `ENOBUFS` fallback to a
copying send. Secure connections are excluded once in
`ProtocolV2::ready()`. RDMA/DPDK/Windows inherit no-ops via default
implementations on `ConnectedSoc

70645.title: common: consolidate string split helpers
70645.author: chardan
70645.body:
Migrates split.h and str_list.h into str_lib.h, with concept-aware
unified behavior. Preserves split() performance and implements the
old str_list functions in terms of it. Iterator behavior is constexpr-capable, 
split can be checked at compile-time (and as much else as I could get to
work at compile-time also does).

Consolidating and modernizing the string split/join helpers was possible
without regressing the split paths, while making joins materially cheaper.

## Performance versus main

As a happy bonus, this process has yielded strong performance improvements:

Median µs/op; GCC 17, `-O3`, Ryzen 9 7900X. Negative changes mean less time.

| Operation | Input | Main | PR | Time change | Allocations, main → PR |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Join | 256 short strings | 1.57 | 1.47 | -7% | 8 → 1 |
| Split → vector | 512 short tokens | 14.40 | 4.79 | -67% | 10 → 1 |
| Split → list | 512 short tokens | 20.37 | 8.69 | -57% | 512 → 512 |
| Borrowed split, delimiter set | 512 short tokens | 1.63 | 1.63 | ~0% | 0 → 0 |
| Borrowed split, char delimiter | 512 short tokens | 1.42 | 2.47 | +74% | 0 → 0 |
| Borrowed split, char delimiter | 128 long tokens | 1.51 | 0.69 | -54% | 0 → 0 |
| Borrowed split, char delimiter | 128 tokens, alternating 6/48 bytes | 0.83 | 0.67 | -20% | 0 → 0 |

Although significant, the single regression affects only the char delimiter overload, used in just two production call sites in rgwadmin's REST API (user creation and modification). Changing from 'c' to "s" triggers the other path, so the single-character overload is now actually never used. (IMO, we can safely remove that overload, although this being C++ it's probably good to be complete...). The regression is caused by the single-character overload resulting in an out-of-line memchr() call. 

(Note: I am guilty of some drive-by style churn here in the call site changes.)

Assisted-by: Codex:GPT-5

Signed-off-by: Jesse F. Williamson <jfw@ibm.com>

70652.title: crimson/os/seastore/async_cleaner: release segments that don't have valid headers
70652.author: xxhdx1985126
70652.body:
When opening a segment, BlockSegmentManager's SegmentStateTracker is
first written out and then the segment header is written. And when
scanning segments on startup, SegmentCleaner determines whether a
segment is empty or closed by detecting a valid segment header. So if
the OSD crashes after the SegmentStateTracker is written out and before
the segment header is written, the segment state in SegmentCleaner and
that in the SegmentStateTracker after OSD reboot will be inconsistent.

This commit resolve this issue by making SegmentCleaner try to release
segments that don't have valid headers, after which the segment states
would be consistent

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/78739
Signed-off-by: Xuehan Xu <xuxuehan@qianxin.com>

70662.title: mon: change mon_config_key_max_entry_size value from 64_k to 256_k
70662.author: aadhikale
70662.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/75346

If we have 375 host entries in mgr/cephadm/inventory (cephadm host inventory), with an average size of approximately 182 bytes per host this value may vary depending on the hostname length as well as the number and size of labels the total inventory size would be approximately 68,250 bytes (375 × 182). This exceeds the default value of mon_config_key_max_entry_size (65,536 bytes).

By increasing mon_config_key_max_entry_size to 1 MB, the inventory could accommodate approximately 5,761 host entries (1,048,576 ÷ 182), providing a significantly larger and safer margin for future growth.

Test before code changes:

./bin/ceph -c ./ceph.conf -k ./keyring config get mon mon_config_key_max_entry_size

65536

Test after code changes:

./bin/ceph -c ./ceph.conf -k ./keyring config get mon mon_config_key_max_entry_size

262144

70668.title: rgw/sts: Add a new envelope format with AES-256-GCM support
70668.author: mheler
70668.body:
Adds a versioned `v2.` session token envelope sealed with AES-256-GCM, which supports non-disruptive key rotations.

Sealing keys live in the mon config-key store at `rgw/sts/keys` and are managed with `radosgw-admin sts keyring init|rotate|list|rm trim`. Up to 16 keys, where the first one seals and the rest verify, so rotating doesn't invalidate outstanding sessions. 

`rgw_sts_token_format` stays `legacy` by default, issuing the existing tokens and accepting both formats. Flip it to `aead` once every gateway has the keyring. The single legacy key can move into the config-key store too, managed with `--legacy`.

Deployment, rotation and rollback are documented in `doc/radosgw/STS.rst`.

Depends on: https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/70538

70698.title: mgr/cephadm: set filesystems joinable immediately after MDS daemons are upgraded
70698.author: ShwetaBhosale1
70698.body:
Previously, after upgrading MDS daemons, the code would return control
    to the serve loop and rely on the next iteration to detect (via cephadm
    cache) that no more MDS daemons need upgrading, then call
    _complete_mds_upgrade(). This added an unnecessary serve loop iteration
    delay before filesystems were set joinable again.
    
    Now, immediately after upgrading MDS daemons, _verify_all_mds_upgraded()
    queries 'ceph versions' to confirm all MDS daemons report the target
    version. If verified, _complete_mds_upgrade() is called right away
    before returning to the serve loop, reducing the window during which
    filesystems remain not-joinable
    
    Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/78826
    Signed-off-by: Shweta Bhosale <Shweta.Bhosale1@ibm.com>

70699.title: rgw/swift: fix ?multipart-manifest=get returning empty body for SLO objects
70699.author: jrse
70699.body:
When GET ?multipart-manifest=get is used on a Static Large Object, RGW returns Content-Length: 0 with an empty body. This is because RGW stores the SLO manifest as a binary-encoded xattr (RGW_ATTR_SLO_MANIFEST) with zero data bytes in the RADOS object. The skip_manifest flag bypasses the SLO handler, falling through to the normal read path which finds no data.

Fix: when skip_manifest is true and the SLO manifest xattr is present, decode the RGWSLOInfo, reconstruct the JSON manifest (raw format with path, etag, size_bytes fields), and return it as the response body with Content-Type: application/json.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/78866

70735.title: kv/RocksDBStore: refuse to open a db with an interrupted resharding, fix repair with extra column families
70735.author: FredNass
70735.body:
Resuming an interrupted resharding with `ceph-bluestore-tool` reshard fails with "extra columns in rocksdb" (#73507), while the man page promises it can always be continued or reverted.

As Adam pointed out, the promise cannot be kept today: BlueStore initializes its allocator from the freelist or the onodes stored in the db, which are only partially visible on a half-resharded db, so resuming could overwrite live data. This PR therefore:

refuses to open a db with an interrupted resharding, read-only included, with an explicit message, and updates the ceph-bluestore-tool man page to say such an OSD has to be redeployed (last commit);
fixes repair mode when RepairDB() has resurrected column families that are not part of the sharding definition: they are now opened and dropped instead of making the db unopenable (Igor's refactoring included, thanks);
adds `read_sharding_def()` and unit tests for both cases.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/73507

Assisted-by: Claude Fable 5 High.

70736.title: os/bluestore: automatically reshard legacy RocksDB databases on mount
70736.author: FredNass
70736.body:
### What problem does it solve and how?

OSDs created prior to Pacific do not use RocksDB column family sharding unless they have been manually migrated with ceph-bluestore-tool reshard, an offline, per-OSD procedure that is tedious on large clusters and takes ages (especially when the failure domain is host and the operator can only proceed with one host at a time).

This adds `bluestore_reshard_db_on_mount` (default: false). When **tru**e, an OSD whose RocksDB database is not sharded yet reshards it to the layout defined by bluestore_rocksdb_cfs at startup, before the store is mounted. A whole cluster can be converted with ceph config set osd bluestore_reshard_db_on_mount true followed by a rolling restart, similar in spirit to bluestore_fsck_quick_fix_on_mount.

### Key points

Reuses the exact ceph-bluestore-tool reshard code path: open_db_environment(&kvdb, false, /*to_repair=*/true) + RocksDBStore::reshard() + close_db_environment(), then _mount() proceeds normally. No new DB-manipulation code. The hook runs before the bluestore_fsck_on_mount block, so a configured fsck validates the post-reshard state.

The decision is based solely on the sharding definition stored in the OSD's own BlueFS, read at mount time under the fsid lock via read_sharding_def() — never on external or cached state. A definition that exists but cannot be read fails the mount instead of being mistaken for "not sharded". 

Even a misfire would only trigger an idempotent reshard: keys already in their target column family are skipped, and the target spec is validated before any mutation.

Free-space pre-flight: old and new copies of the data coexist in BlueFS until the old CFs are dropped, so resharding only starts if free space on the db+slow devices covers the current db footprint plus 20% slack (spillover space included). If short, the OSD logs an error and continues running non-sharded — no crash loop.

### Interruption

As with the offline tool, the resharding must not be interrupted: an interrupted resharding cannot be safely resumed (see #70735 and Adam's analysis there), and the OSD then has to be redeployed. The documentation recommends setting noout and restarting one host at a time so that such a failure stays within what the replication tolerates. This is the same exposure as the manual procedure; the option only automates the trigger.

### New test

StoreTestSpecificAUSize.BluestoreReshardDBOnMountTest — creates a non-sharded store (bluestore_rocksdb_cf=false, as mkfs'd before Pacific), writes object data + omap, remounts with the option set, verifies the sharding definition was applied and data/omap survived, and that a second remount is a no-op.

### Documentation and releate note updates

Also updates the "RocksDB Sharding" section of the BlueStore configuration reference and adds a release note.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/78901

Assisted-by: Claude Fable 5 High.

70758.title: tentacle: mgr/cephadm: don't let a non-RSA key kill the serve loop
70758.author: tchaikov
70758.body:
pyOpenSSL's PKey.check() only understands RSA and raises TypeError for anything else:
```
    File "OpenSSL/crypto.py", line 414, in check
      raise TypeError("Only RSA keys can currently be checked.")
    TypeError: Only RSA keys can currently be checked.
```
`verify_tls()` caught (`ValueError`, `crypto.Error`), so storing an EC certificate/key pair let that `TypeError` escape all the way out of `_check_certificates()`, which runs early in the cephadm serve loop. The module then failed with `MGR_MODULE_ERROR`, every "ceph orch" command stopped working, and the same crash recurred on each mgr restart.

Limit `check()` to RSA keys instead of dropping it. `load_privatekey()` does not verify that an RSA key is internally consistent, so `check()` is doing real work: of 200 bit-flipped keys fed through the PEM path, 198 parsed fine and were rejected only by check(). Non-RSA keys are still validated against the certificate by `check_privatekey()`.

Also catch the general case in `_check_certificate_state()`, so a future crypto backend failure marks one certificate invalid instead of taking down the orchestrator.

This is not a cherry-pick from main because the offending code no longer exists there. d814088ce7d reimplemented `InternalCryptoCaller` on top of cryptography and dropped pyOpenSSL, which removed the `PKey.check()` call and fixed this as a side effect. That rewrite replaces every method in the class and is not suitable for a stable branch, so the RSA assumption is fixed in place here instead.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/78939

70763.title: cephadm: defer set-user call until after SSH key registration
70763.author: rsacherer
70763.body:
During bootstrap, prepare_ssh() called 'cephadm set-user' as its very first operation, before any SSH key was registered with the mgr.  The mgr's set_ssh_user handler invokes _validate_and_set_ssh_val which calls _reconfig_ssh(); RHCS 9.1 / Squid enforces that a public key must exist before the user can be changed, so the call fails immediately with:

  Error EINVAL: No SSH public key configured. Please generate or set SSH
  keys first using ceph cephadm generate-key or ceph cephadm set-pub-key.

Fix: move cli(['cephadm', 'set-user', ...]) to after the if/elif/else key-setup block in prepare_ssh(), so it is always called after keys are registered regardless of which path is taken (provided keys, signed cert, or auto-generated key).

Verified on RHEL 9.8 + rhceph-9-rhel9:latest (ceph 20.2.1-324.el9cp):
- buggy binary: bootstrap fails at prepare_ssh with the EINVAL above
- patched binary: bootstrap completes, ssh-user set successfully

Three unit tests added to TestPrepareSsh in test_cephadm.py: ordering checks for the provided-keys and generate-key paths, plus a strict mock that fires the exact EINVAL if set-user precedes key setup.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/78943
Signed-off-by: Raimund Sacherer <rsachere@redhat.com>

70765.title: mgr/alerts: add PagerDuty support
70765.author: liewegas
70765.body:
## Summary

Extend the `alerts` mgr module to open, update, and resolve incidents in PagerDuty via the Events API v2, in parallel with the existing SMTP delivery.

Each Ceph health check maps to a separate PagerDuty incident, deduplicated by check code (prefixed by the cluster fsid so a single routing key can be shared across clusters):

- new check → `trigger`
- check count increased → `trigger` again (same dedup key updates the incident)
- cleared check → `resolve`

`HEALTH_ERR` maps to severity `critical`, `HEALTH_WARN` to `warning`. An on-demand `ceph alerts send` re-triggers all currently active checks so PagerDuty state is reconciled with the cluster.

### New module options

| Option | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pagerduty_routing_key` | *(empty)* | PagerDuty integration/routing key; PagerDuty is disabled when unset |
| `pagerduty_url` | `https://events.pagerduty.com/v2/enqueue` | Events API endpoint |
| `pagerduty_source` | *(cluster fsid)* | Event `source` field |
| `pagerduty_component` | `ceph` | Event `component` field |
| `pagerduty_timeout` | `10s` | Per-request timeout |

Failures to reach PagerDuty are surfaced as an `ALERTS_PAGERDUTY_ERROR` health check, mirroring the existing `ALERTS_SMTP_ERROR` pattern. Only stdlib (`http.client`, `urllib.parse`) is used — no new dependencies.

Docs updated in `doc/mgr/alerts.rst` with a new "PagerDuty" section.

## Test plan

- [ ] Enable alerts module, set `pagerduty_routing_key` on a live cluster, generate a health warning, and confirm an incident is opened.
- [ ] Increase the count of an active check and confirm the incident is updated (not duplicated).
- [ ] Clear the check and confirm the incident is auto-resolved.
- [ ] Run `ceph alerts send` and confirm all active checks are re-triggered idempotently (dedup-key stable).
- [ ] Set `pagerduty_url` to an unreachable host and confirm `ALERTS_PAGERDUTY_ERROR` appears in `ceph health detail` and the mgr thread is not blocked past the timeout.

70780.title: mds: preserve request errors in file blockdiff
70780.author: LiShengG
70780.body:
`LIST_SNAPS` on an absent object returns `-ENOENT` at the request level,
while decoding its empty per-op payload records `-EIO`.
`file_blockdiff()` previously retained only the per-op result, causing
`aggregate_snap_sets()` to reject sparse-file holes and abort incremental
CephFS snapshot synchronization.

Preserve the request-level error when the Objecter request fails. This
keeps absent objects reported as `-ENOENT`, while decoder failures from
otherwise successful requests remain `-EIO`.

Add a cephfs-mirror regression test that creates a sparse file containing
absent objects and verifies its incremental snapshot synchronization.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/78964

## Test coverage

Added `TestMirroring.test_cephfs_mirror_sparse_file_sync` to cover
incremental synchronization of a sparse file with multiple absent data
objects.

70794.title: os/bluestore: implement claim_range()
70794.author: Naveenaidu
70794.body:
Closes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/76421

### NOTE:

This PR depends on the PR https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/71656 to be merged. That PR fixes some lookup bugs in BtreeAllocator and Btree2Allocator which becomes evident when used with claim_range

## Brief Explanation

Currently `BlueStore::Allocator::allocate()` accepts a hint, but it is purely advisory, the allocator is free to ignore it. There is no way to take a specific range of disk space atomically. This is required for a future lazy discard policy.

Discards and Release are currently tightly coupled in `BlueStore::_txc_release_alloc`. The released space is not immediately usable by `allocate()` until the discard has happened. This coupling is wasteful as the space that got discarded might get reused anyway - wasting precious compute and time. Lazy discard wants to flip this: we want to release immediately (space reusable right away), and defer/batch the actual discard. 

When the discard thread is ready to act on a released range, that range may still be free, may be fully re-allocated (re-used by new writes), or partially both. The equivalent `foreach() + init_rm_free()` sequence has a window between the two calls in which free space can be given away by a concurrent `allocate()`.

For example:

```
(T0): space is released
(T1): space reused by a new write 
(T2): deferred discard finally fires
```

A discard issued at T2 based on stale info would wipe out the T1 write's live data. 

`claim_range()` closes this: right before firing the deferred discard, atomically re-claim whatever part of the range is *still* free (excluding whatever got reused), and only discard that returned sub-range.

This PR adds `claim_range(offset, length, *extents)` as a pure virtual on Allocator. It atomically marks the entire `[offset, offset+length)` range as allocated under the allocator lock, and reports back only the sub-ranges that were previously free (i.e. what was actually newly claimed). Already-allocated parts are untouched. Unlike `init_rm_free()`, `claim_range()` never asserts on state: any mix of free and allocated space in the range is legal input.

In future, one can use this function like so:

```
discard(start, end):
   extents <- claim_range(start, end)
   actual_discard(extents)
```

## Implementation

  claim_range() is implemented for all six in-tree backends:

  - AvlAllocator — thin wrapper around _try_remove_from_tree()
  - BtreeAllocator — same shape, after fixing _try_remove_from_tree() bugs
  - Btree2Allocator — same shape, after fixing _try_remove_from_tree() bugs
  - BitmapAllocator — new walk over the L0/L1/L2 bitmap hierarchy
  - StupidAllocator — adapted from init_rm_free(), drops the state assert, fixes num_free accounting
  - HybridAllocator — delegates to primary tree + fallback bitmap

---

## Testing

#### Goal: Real life testing of `Allocator::claim_range()` that runs alongside a live Bluestore and spams `claim_range` on the main allocator. `ClaimRangeStressThread` does this. In order to be confident of the results of this test we had to do two things:

1. Claims must in majority come back partial, i.e the range claim_range works on should have a mixture of free and allocated space. This will help us find if buggy `claim_range` can hand out live spaces.
2. The test actually fails when we have a bug, We broke `claim_range` on purpose and checked that the run fails.

In order to know how the stress thread find bugs, please read the commit message: https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/70794/changes/c91a437263e7a8dcab2c25d1ee80eae5a2258ec2

One thing to note, at every umount the stress thread logs a summary line, this will help us detect the setup and the problem:
```
claims full F partial P zero Z sentinels edge E middle M claimed X released Y
```

The tests were run at the default settings of the new configuration we added. Notably few:
* `claim_length`: 64 MiB
* `max_claims`: 16
* `ma

70798.title: test/osd: add op scheduler isolation benchmarks
70798.author: mmgaggle
70798.body:
Isolation benchmarks for the OSD op schedulers, split out of #70627 per @markhpc's suggestion so they can land independently and be used against the existing schedulers. Everything here is scheduler agnostic: the harness takes an `op_queue_type_t` and drives whatever `make_scheduler()` returns, so a new scheduler is covered by adding it to a type list — which is exactly what the bfq RFC now does on top of this.

Two tiers:

**Tier 1 — `ceph_bench_op_scheduler`** (in-process): drives identical synthetic workloads through wpq and mclock, pacing dequeues at a simulated device rate. mclock's capacity options are calibrated to the same rate and its future-time dequeue results are honored, so scenarios run in real time. Streams model client sessions via distinct owners; metrics are per-stream share, throughput, and sojourn-time percentiles. Scenarios: victim share vs aggressor session fan-out (1..16), paced-victim latency under a saturating aggressor, and client-vs-recovery class weighting.

Representative results at 100 MB/s simulated, one victim client vs an aggressor fanning out over K sessions (both saturating):

| K sessions | wpq victim share | mclock victim share |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 50.0% | 50.3% |
| 4 | 20.0% | 20.1% |
| 16 | 5.9% | 6.7% |

Both schedulers dilute the victim as 1/(K+1): wpq round-robins owners, and mclock maps all client ops to a single dmclock client (`client_profile_id_t` is always default-constructed), so neither can hold a per-workload share as session count scales. A paced victim offered 20% of the device under a saturating 8-session aggressor: mclock delivers the offered 20 MB/s but at p99 419 ms (FIFO behind the aggressor backlog); wpq caps the victim below its offered rate (11 MB/s) at p99 1.3 s. Client-vs-recovery follows each scheduler's own dial: mclock 50/50 per the balanced profile, wpq 79/21 by priority tokens.

**Tier 2 — `src/test/osd/vstart_bench_scheduler.sh`**: the same isolation matrix with real `rados bench` clients against a single-OSD, single-op-shard vstart cluster, cycling `osd_op_queue` per cell; reports victim bandwidth and latency plus a mid-cell `dump_op_pq_state` snapshot. The script header documents the two things that otherwise silently invalidate the experiment on fast devices: constraining `bluestore_throttle_bytes` (default 4 MiB here) so contention actually surfaces at the op queue rather than being absorbed by BlueStore, and giving the victim enough queue depth that it does not self-cap below its fair share (Little's law; default QD=64).

`unittest_scheduler_isolation` carries harness sanity checks (work conservation, no outright starvation of equal streams). It skips unless `CEPH_TEST_SCHEDULER_ISOLATION` is set, because the harness paces in wall time and shared CI executors are too noisy for that.

70805.title: [RFC] doc/dev: add RBD Orbital Snapshots design doc
70805.author: mmgaggle
70805.body:
This is an RFC for **Orbital Snapshots**: archiving RBD snapshots to S3-compatible object storage as a shared regional snapshot tier — incremental push, instant-live restore via image live migration, and a snapshot lineage that any cluster can continue.

The target deployment is N per-AZ Ceph clusters sharing one regional object store: EBS-snapshot semantics for RBD. This is explicitly *not* a low-RPO DR mechanism — recovery points are snapshot-granularity. It competes with "we run rbd-mirror because there was no other option", not with mirroring itself, and with `export`/`export-diff` pipelines, whose sequential streams cannot back a live restore.

Design highlights (full spec in the doc):

- One S3 object per RADOS object under deterministic lineage-scoped keys; no exhaustive manifest.
- A per-snapshot layer is a small JSON header plus a 2-bit-per-object bitmap (`ceph::BitVector<2>`, the object-map encoding): EXISTS / INHERITED / ZEROED, with clone-style fall-through along the layer chain (~650 KiB of metadata per snapshot of a 10 TiB image).
- Restore is a new `orbital` format in `librbd/migration` beside `raw` and `qcow`: `rbd migration prepare` yields an instantly-usable image, and background hydration answers `list_snaps` from bitmap diffs, so it fetches exactly the objects each snapshot references.
- Portable incrementals: a transient snapshot plus server-side CRC32C (OSD CHECKSUM op) compared against a checksum sidecar — no common snapshot needed between clusters, which `export-diff` cannot do.
- Concurrent writers are fenced by a per-lineage HEAD pointer updated with S3 conditional PUT (ETag CAS); forks stay representable, like a clone tree.
- Layer deletion/compaction is librbd flatten transplanted to S3: server-side `CopyObject` as copyup, no data through the client.
- Dependency split: aws-sdk-cpp in the `rbd` CLI only (write side); the librbd read path keeps the lightweight `HttpClient`/`S3Stream`, upgraded from SigV2 to a self-contained SigV4 signer, so the SDK never enters qemu's link graph.

Feedback particularly wanted on:

- implementing restore as a migration format vs a new first-class mechanism
- appetite for aws-sdk-cpp as a tool-side dependency
- whether the HEAD-pointer fencing / fork model is sufficient
- CLI surface (`rbd orbital push/pull` vs something more conservative)

A discussion thread on dev@ceph.io will follow.

Assisted-by: claude:claude-fable-5

70827.title: common,exporter: Add 1D Perf Histograms (for Prometheus)
70827.author: irq0
70827.body:
This series makes perf counter histograms available in Prometheus. It adds the capability; RGW is the first user of it in a separate PR.

PerfHistogram gains everything needed for that: 
 - 1D histograms get builder and hinc() overloads
 - Axis now track a rolling sum (Prometheus _sum)
 - Axis can declare explicit inclusive boundaries. There is also a convenience constructor for Prometheus' default latency buckets.
 - Each axis records its units, so exporters can convert easily
 - A new add_time_histogram + htinc helps with working with latency measurements 


`counter {dump,schema}` learn a histograms flag, and the Ceph Exporter turns 1D histograms into Prometheus histogram families. A scrape with exporter_histograms = true then yields:


```
# HELP ceph_rgw_op_hist_lat_seconds Request latency distribution
# TYPE ceph_rgw_op_hist_lat_seconds histogram
ceph_rgw_op_hist_lat_seconds_bucket{instance_id="8000",le="0",op="put_obj"} 0
ceph_rgw_op_hist_lat_seconds_bucket{instance_id="8000",le="0.005",op="put_obj"} 0
ceph_rgw_op_hist_lat_seconds_bucket{instance_id="8000",le="0.01",op="put_obj"} 0
```

70840.title: rgw,common: replace no-op MD5 FIPS flag with explicit MD5NonCrypto type
70840.author: MarkAtwood
70840.body:
rgw computes MD5 in 31 places that are not cryptography: S3/Swift ETags, cache
keys, short zone-id hashes. Each has to be tagged by hand with
`SetFlags(EVP_MD_CTX_FLAG_NON_FIPS_ALLOW)` to survive a FIPS configuration.
This replaces the flag with a type, `ceph::crypto::MD5NonCrypto`.

The flag does not do what its name says. `EVP_MD_CTX_FLAG_NON_FIPS_ALLOW` was
only ever read by the OpenSSL 1.x FIPS module; 3.0 keeps the macro and ignores
it. The sites that set it work because `OpenSSLDigest::SetFlags` intercepts the
flag and re-fetches MD5 with a `fips=no` property query.

Being a separate statement after construction, it is also easy to forget.
Four sites never got it:

* `ETagVerifier_MPU`: the constructor flags the base class's `hash` a second
  time and never its own `mpu_etag_hash`
* `DBMultipartUpload::complete` in `rgw_sal_dbstore.cc`: same etag-of-etags
  pattern, no flag at all
* the bucket-logging object-commit ETag in `rgw_sal_rados.cc`
* the AWS `md5` checksum type in `rgw_cksum_digest.h` (`TDigest<ceph::crypto::MD5>`)

Under a strict FIPS configuration (default property query `fips=yes`) those
four crash radosgw. `Restart()` ignores the `EVP_DigestInit_ex` return value,
so `ctx->digest` is left NULL and the next `Update()` sends `EVP_DigestUpdate`
down its legacy branch into a NULL `ctx->update`. Measured on OpenSSL 3.0.13
with only the default provider loaded; no FIPS module is needed to reproduce,
since a `fips=yes` query already fails to resolve MD5.

A type cannot be forgotten. `MD5NonCrypto` fetches MD5 with an explicit
`fips=no` query, cached for process lifetime, falling back to `EVP_md5()`;
below 3.0 it is `EVP_md5()` with `EVP_MD_CTX_FLAG_NON_FIPS_ALLOW` set on the context before init, which RHEL 8's patched 1.1.1 honors in FIPS mode. The second commit converts the 27 flagged sites
and the 4 unflagged ones; the third deletes `SetFlags` and the `mpType_FIPS`
plumbing.

Digest bytes are unchanged, so ETags stay wire-identical. The only behavior
difference is in FIPS mode, where those four sites stop crashing.

API impact: `OpenSSLDigest::SetFlags()` is removed, rgw held the only callers.
`complete_etag()` now takes `MD5NonCrypto&`, and `RGWEtag`'s user-declared
constructor is deleted, it existed only to hold the flag block. I can add a
deprecated `SetFlags` alias rather than remove it outright, if you prefer.

Two things deliberately left out. The `-Wdeprecated-declarations` pragmas stay:
they still cover the `HMAC` class, whose `HMAC_CTX_*` calls are
`OSSL_DEPRECATEDIN_3_0` on 3.x, so they cannot go until `HMAC` moves to
`EVP_MAC`. (#70125's commit message said they would come out with this PR; that
was wrong.) And `Restart()`/`Final()` still discard their return values, which
is why these sites crash rather than error. Fixing that lets the constructor
throw, so every construction site needs an audit first. Happy to fold either in.

The fips=yes test is its own binary, `unittest_ceph_crypto_fips`, so ctest runs it
in a separate process and the default-property change can't leak into other tests.

Testing: 20.2.2-based package build clean, radosgw up and serving. Single-PUT
ETag matched `md5sum`; multipart (5+5+3 MiB) ETag matched an independent Python
`hashlib` etag-of-etags, every part ETag equal. A standalone harness anchors
`MD5NonCrypto` against the RFC 1321 vectors under both the default and a
`fips=yes` property query, and confirms the old flagged path produces identical
bytes.

70847.title: os/bluestore: Fix hanging Collection::flush()
70847.author: aclamk
70847.body:
The testing showed that sometimes BlueStore::OpSequencer::flush() hangs.

A script that replicates the problem (sometimes, patience needed).

```
\#!/bin/bash
\# best execute from /dev/shm
export CBIN=/home/akupczyk/ceph-2/build/

for ((t=0; t<20; t++))
do
  {
  for ((i=0; i<100; i++))
  do
    rm log$t.txt
    rm out$t.$i.txt
    ${CBIN}/bin/ceph_test_objectstore --gtest_filter=\*BlueStore\*Matrix\* \
      --bluestore_debug_enforce_settings=ssd --debug_rocksdb=0/0 --plugin_dir=${CBIN}/lib \
      --log_to_stderr=false --log_file=log$t.txt > out$t.$i.txt 2>&1 || exit
    echo THREAD $t ITERATION $i DONE
  done
  } &
done
wait
echo ALL DONE
```

The captures hangs show all transactions in sequencer in STATE_DONE, and a thread waiting on
```
  void flush() {
    ...
    qcond.wait(l);
    ...
  }
```

I was unable to find exact execution sequence that leads to the hang. The path I suspected was that flush() sleeps waiting on qcong for youngest transaction to progress further than STATE_KV_SUBMITTED, but that transaction was able to pass through execution without signalling qcond.

Actions:
1) Added locks around `qcond.notify_all()`.
2) Moved to `qcond.wait(.., predicate)`

70881.title: cephfs_mirror: Fix files with restored mtime in incremental sync
70881.author: kotreshhr
70881.body:
The mirror doesn't sync a file during incremental sync if the
 file is modified and mtime is restored between two snapshots.

 Fix is to use mtime|ctime|size as a mask in open_snapdiff which would
 report files whose content changed between snapshots when mtime is
 restored. Mask 0 defaults to mtime-only and misses that case.

 Also, should_sync_entry needs to accomodate ctime, since it can
 miss same size file modification with preserved mtime.

 Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/77892
 Signed-off-by: Kotresh HR <khiremat@redhat.com>

70883.title: cmake: share bundled Boost source across build dirs via WITH_BOOST_CACHE
70883.author: JBakamovic
70883.body:
When building the bundled Boost (WITH_SYSTEM_BOOST=OFF), every out-of-source build directory independently downloads a ~126MB tarball, extracts it (~79k files), and builds the b2 engine before compiling Boost. Maintaining several build directories for the same Boost version repeats all of this setup per directory, which is wasteful.

Add an opt-in `WITH_BOOST_CACHE=<directory>` that points at a shared, version-partitioned Boost source cache. The tarball is downloaded, extracted, and used to build the b2 engine there exactly once, at configure time and under a file lock (so concurrent cold configures are serialized). Every build directory of that Boost version then reuses the cache read-only: the ExternalProject download/extract step disappears from the build graph entirely.

Only the source is shared; variant-specific artifacts are never written back into the cache:

  - b2 builds out of the source tree via --build-dir/--stagedir, so objects and staged libs land under the build dir's own boost-artifacts/, leaving the shared source pristine and safe for concurrent/parallel builds.
  - The expected ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/boost/{include,lib} layout that downstream consumers (Arrow, OpenTelemetry) and the imported targets rely on is provided by symlinks - headers point back at the cache, libs at this build's staged libs - so nothing is duplicated (in particular the ~180MB header tree is not re-copied per build dir).
  - The real bootstrap.sh is run out-of-source (cwd = build dir, --with-bjam reusing the cached engine), emitting project-config.jam into the build dir. Platform detection (ICU discovery, etc.) and library selection come straight from the upstream script rather than being reimplemented in CMake, so this stays correct across Boost versions and platforms.

This does not make a single build's Boost compile faster - compiling Boost costs essentially the same whether the setup runs at configure or at build time (compiled libraries are variant-specific and are not shared). The gain is not repeating the one-time setup - download, extraction and the serial, single-threaded b2 engine build - in every build directory, plus not duplicating the source tree or header tree. The payoff therefore scales with the number of build directories in play.

Benefits most: workflows with several build directories of one Boost version (e.g. debug/release/asan/ubsan/backport/agentic (work)trees), frequent fresh out-of-source builds, or CI matrices building many configurations. Default behavior is unchanged: with the flag unset, the existing per-build download-and-build path is used verbatim, and the src/boost submodule path is untouched. The feature relies on shell/symlink support and is therefore Unix-only.

Signed-off-by: Jusufadis Bakamovic <jusufadis.bakamovic@clyso.com>
