72827.title: auth: read back the pending key that KeyRing prints
72827.author: tchaikov
72827.body:
KeyRing::print() writes an entity's pending key as a "pending key" line, so "ceph auth get" and "ceph auth export" include it while a rotation is pending. KeyRing::set_modifier() does not know that name and rejects it. A file saved from that output then fails to load as a client keyring, with "ceph auth import -i" and with "ceph-authtool -l":
```
  error setting modifier for [client.foo] type=pending key val=...:
  Malformed input
```
Accept "pending key" and store it as the entry's pending key, so an export and import round trip keeps both keys. Clients still authenticate with "key" only, so this does not change which key a client uses.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81871

72828.title: cls/user: reset_user_stats2 continues from the accumulated stats
72828.author: fa-at-pulsit
72828.body:
`radosgw-admin user stats --reset-stats` (and `account stats --reset-stats`) rebuilds the user header stats with several `reset_user_stats2` calls of up to 1000 bucket entries each. The client passes the stats accumulated so far, but the cls method never used them. So with more than 1000 buckets, the header kept only the stats of the last call: for example 500 instead of 2500 buckets.

The fix starts each call from `op.acc_stats`. Every client since 25a82ed3795 already passes them, so the fix is safe with mixed client and OSD versions.

The new test in `test_cls_user.cc` adds 2500 bucket entries, clears the header stats and rebuilds them with the same call loop as rgw's `reset_stats()`.

This came up while testing #66501, as discussed there (review thread at `cls_user.cc:506`).

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81896

72829.title: include/ceph_releases.h: fix to_string(-1)
72829.author: MaxKellermann
72829.body: A comment in this header says "we used to use -1 for invalid release". This number is (usuallu) represented in the `uint8_t` as `0xff`, and casting the enum to `int` passes this `0xff` instead of `-1`, causing to_string() to return "unknown" instead of "unspecified".

72831.author: MaxKellermann
72831.body: read_header() encoded its `otp_header*` parameter into the bufferlist before reading into it.  Since there is no encoder for pointers, this silently used the bool overload, writing one byte which was then overwritten by cls_cxx_map_get_val() anyway.

72834.title: rgw/dedup: encode urgent_msg_t explicitly as its underlying type
72834.author: MaxKellermann
72834.body: urgent_msg_t is an unscoped enum without an encoder; it was implicitly promoted to int and encoded with the legacy encode(int32_t) overload. Use std::to_underlying() instead, so the wire format does not depend on implicit conversions.  The underlying type is `unsigned int`, which is encoded as the same 4 little-endian bytes (the receiver in Background::handle_notify() decodes an int32_t).

72835.title: test/rbd_mirror: encode MirrorMode explicitly as its underlying type
72835.author: MaxKellermann
72835.body: cls::rbd::MirrorMode is an unscoped enum without an encoder; the mock mirror_mode_get implementation only compiled because the enumerators were implicitly promoted to int and encoded with the legacy encode(int32_t) overload.  Use std::to_underlying() instead; the underlying type is `unsigned int`, which matches the uint32_t that the real cls method encodes and the client decodes.

72836.title: include/health: fix parameter type of denc_traits<health_status_t>::b…
72836.author: MaxKellermann
72836.body:
…ound_encode()

The parameter was `const ceph::buffer::ptr&` instead of `const health_status_t&`.  This only compiled because the enum was implicitly converted to `unsigned` and then to a buffer::ptr via its implicit `ptr(unsigned)` constructor, allocating a temporary buffer of 0..2 bytes on every bound_encode() call.

72837.title: osdc/Objecter: pass the encoded attributes in ObjectOperation::setxat…
72837.author: MaxKellermann
72837.body:
…trs()

setxattrs() encoded the attribute map into `bl`, but then passed `bl.length()` instead of `bl` to add_xattr(), which was implicitly converted to an empty buffer::list via its `list(unsigned prealloc)` constructor, so the attributes were never sent.

This regression was caused 17 years ago by commit 7a624a4a8a449 ("osd: hold op data on the specific op") which removed the "valuelen" overload of add_xattr().  Nobody ever noticed that bug because this is dead code.

72838.title: include/buffer.h: make the unsigned constructors of ptr and list expl…
72838.author: MaxKellermann
72838.body:
…icit

Constructing a buffer::ptr or a buffer::list from an `unsigned` (allocation length / preallocation size) was allowed implicitly, which means any integer could silently be converted to an empty buffer, e.g. when passed to a function taking a buffer::ptr or buffer::list parameter.

Both use KeyValueDB/RocksDBStore code from libkv, but only got it transitively through `os`, which links `kv` only via bluestore. With WITH_BLUESTORE=OFF, they fail to link.  Commit 9a0e3c70c13 fixed the same problem for the other ObjectMap tests.

72840.title: mgr/smb: Add persistent handles availability configuration
72840.author: anoopcs9
72840.body:
Add persistent handle availability configuration for CephFS backed SMB shares, including inheritance, share overrides, durability policies and performance warnings.

Key considerations:
- Disabled by default; supported only for CephFS shares.
- Global support stays enabled while the default or any CephFS share requires it - even with no shares or all shares opting out of an enabled default.
- Cluster defaults use `share_defaults.availability.persistent_handles`. Individual shares override this through `availability.persistent_handles`.
- Global support can only be enabled before the cluster's first orchestration and cannot be re-enabled after disabling. smbd opens its locking databases with per-record persistence only at startup, so enabling it with just a config reload would advertise persistent handles that smbd cannot store. Disabling with just a reload is safe.
- To replace the last share that enables persistent handles, remove it and add the new share in the same `apply`. An enabled cluster default keeps global support reserved even without shares.
- Cluster field `persistent_handles_durability: {full_outage (default) | partial_outage}` can be changed before first orchestration submission, including in the batch adding the first share. Changes are rejected after submission or when orchestration history is unknown. It only matters with persistent handles and clustering enabled.
- Disabling does not revoke existing handles or restart the service. After first orchestration submission, disabling the final persistent-handle requirement warns that global support cannot be re-enabled. Before first submission, disabling remains reversible.

Availability and durability are configured declaratively through cluster and share resources using `ceph smb apply`.

- `mgr/smb: Keep orchestrating clusters without shares` fixes an existing bug where cluster changes stopped reaching a still deployed service once its last share was removed. It also records the orchestration history that the enablement check relies on.
- `mgr/smb: Serialize resource apply operations` and `mgr/smb: Use indexed lookup when collecting cluster shares` are independent of the feature itself.

Here's a sample resource exercising the newly introduced fields.
```yaml
- resource_type: ceph.smb.cluster
  cluster_id: demo
  auth_mode: user
  user_group_settings:
    - source_type: resource
      ref: smb-users
  persistent_handles_durability: partial_outage
  share_defaults:
    availability:
      persistent_handles: true

# Inherits persistent handles from the cluster's share defaults.
- resource_type: ceph.smb.share
  cluster_id: demo
  share_id: available
  cephfs:
    volume: cephfs
    path: /available

# Explicitly opts out without disabling global support.
- resource_type: ceph.smb.share
  cluster_id: demo
  share_id: ordinary
  cephfs:
    volume: cephfs
    path: /ordinary
  availability:
    persistent_handles: false
```

depends on #72443

72852.title: rgw: reload when the period changed while the gateway started
72852.author: lumir-sliva
72852.body:
## Summary

A radosgw that is still starting when a new period reaches its zone can miss the realm reload and keep running the old period until it's restarted. With more than one gateway per zone, another gateway takes the period push, stores it and notifies, while the starting one isn't watching the realm yet. If the change made the starting gateway's zone the master, the zone that was master before never hears about it either.

## Problem

Startup order (`rgw_appmain.cc` at ce66551f120):

- `init_storage()` loads the realm and its current period (`site.load()`, line 301). The gateway runs with that period until its next reload.
- `init_frontends2()` starts the frontends (line 619), so the gateway already takes requests, period pushes included.
- Only then is the realm watch set up (`create_realm_watcher()`, line 639, `watch2()` in `realm_watcher.cc:101`), and the period pusher and the reload handler are added after that (`add_watcher(...)`, lines 642 and 661).

A period change in between is stored in rados but doesn't reload this gateway:

- a notify before `watch2()` reaches no watcher;
- one between `watch2()` and `add_watcher()` finds no handler and is dropped: "Failed to find a watcher for notify type 1" (`realm_watcher.cc:64`);
- a later push of the same period stops at "already have epoch" in `RGWOp_Period_Post` (`rgw_rest_realm.cc:172-178`) and returns 200 without notifying.

`RGWRealmReloader::reload()` already guards against this for a reload in progress (`rgw_realm_reloader.cc:110`, "or we could miss some updates"); startup doesn't.

The notify carries two things, `ZonesNeedPeriod` for the period pusher and `Reload` for the reloader (`driver/rados/config/realm.cc`, `realm_notify_new_period`). Both are lost. The pusher built in `init_frontends2()` reads the period the driver started with (`rgw_period_pusher.cc:177`), so when the change in the window promoted this zone to master, nobody pushes the new period to the old master: it keeps running as master until the next commit.

Found with `test_multi_period_incremental_sync_backlog` from #72670 at 3 zones x 2 gateways: 5 of 5 runs fail because one of zone 3's gateways never reloads after the zone restarts. The test sleeps `reconfigure_delay` (5 s) and starts zone 3's gateways one after the other, and the master's period pusher retries at +2 s and +6 s, so the +6 s retry lands between the two starts every time.

## Fix

Once the last init step is done, `AppMain::reload_if_period_changed()` reads the realm's current period and its latest epoch again. If either differs from what `init_storage()` loaded, it does what the lost notify would have done, in the same order: it hands the period to the period pusher, which sends it on to the zones that still need it when this zone is its master, and schedules a reload. A zone that the current period did not contain yet runs on its local zonegroup, which is how a new zone starts out; for it, the check reloads once the current period contains the zone. The epoch matters too: an epoch-only change (a zonegroup or zone modify) goes through the reflect path and notifies the same way.

The check runs from `main()` and `RGWLib::init()` after the last init step, not inside `init_frontends2()`, because the reload replaces `env.driver` and `RGWLib::init()` still runs `init_lua()` and `init_dedup()` against it after `init_frontends2()` returns. It compares against a record of what `init_storage()` loaded rather than against the site configuration, which a reload that a notify triggered in the meantime may already be rewriting; if such a reload already loaded the new period, the check schedules one more, which is harmless. `RGWRealmReloader::schedule_reload()` is split out of `handle_notify()` for this, and the reloader keeps its `CephContext` instead of reading it through `env.driver`.

The second commit adds `rgw_inject_delay_pattern=delay_realm_watch`, which holds a starting gateway with its frontends up but before it watches the realm, un

72853.title: osd/ECTransaction: truncate padded shards of legacy EC objects
72853.author: tchaikov
72853.body:
Without EC optimizations, every shard of an EC object is padded to the stripe boundary. After allow_ec_optimizations is set on the pool, truncate() only shrinks the shards whose optimized size, computed from the old object size, is larger than the new one. The other shards keep the legacy padding, so scrub finds them too long and flags the object inconsistent.

With 4+2 and 4K chunks, all six shards of a 20K object are 8K. Truncate it to 16K, and shards 1-3 stay at 8K instead of 4K. RBD hits this when a discard or write-zeroes reaches the end of an object, since librbd sends that as a truncate. With more than m shards flagged, "ceph pg repair" marks them all missing and the object ends up unfound, while its data was fine.

So truncate the remaining shards to their new size as well. Objects written with EC optimizations already have that size. Extending the rollback clone to cover the padding instead doesn't work: the primary doesn't know how long it is, and BlueStore rejects a clone_range past the end of an object.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81915

Use folded block scalar to parse the echo command with hash correctly. Silences an error e-mail to PR reviewers.

Fixes GH check error:
```console
Run echo "review by @${REVIEWER} on
/home/runner/work/_temp/2e76cf23-7785-4efe-acd1-a779a873c05d.sh: line 1: unexpected EOF while looking for matching `"'

72856.title: .github: fix YAML comment truncation
72856.author: dparmar18
72856.body:
e.g.:
```
Run echo "review by @${REVIEWER} on
  echo "review by @${REVIEWER} on
  shell: /usr/bin/bash -e {0}
  env:
    REVIEWER: dparmar18
    PR_NUMBER: 71643
/home/runner/work/_temp/933b85a8-a66d-4c83-88a1-a8bbcf878c0d.sh: line 1: unexpected EOF while looking for matching `"'
Error: Process completed with exit code 2.
```

An unquoted ' #' in a plain scalar starts a YAML comment, everything with it is discarded before anything else sees the value.

Switch to using a block scalar for the run step and quote run-name.

72857.title: .github: quote values containing " #" in reviewer-githubmap.yml
72857.author: tchaikov
72857.body:
YAML treats " #" in an unquoted value as the start of a comment, which cut the PR number off the run-name and left the step with 'echo "review by @... on'. Bash rejects that unterminated quote, so the job fails on every submitted review:
```
  /home/runner/work/_temp/1a4f2074-deb7-4e26-853a-64e893f5a704.sh: line 1: unexpected EOF while looking for matching `"'
  Error: Process completed with exit code 2.
```
`reviewer-githubmap-comment.yml` only runs after this job succeeds, and reads the PR number from the run name, so it stopped posting the .githubmap reminder as well.

Quote both values.

72860.title: mds: count only main-LRU dentries for the trim after an export
72860.author: xiubli
72860.body:
After exporting a subtree, export_finish() calls trim() with the number of dentries that finish_export_dir() handed over, to drop them from the cache right away.  That number includes the null dentries, but clear_auth() has already moved those to the bottom LRU.  trim_lru() empties the bottom LRU without counting it against the count, and then expires the full count from the main LRU.  So every export of a dirfrag full of null dentries, as mass unlinks leave behind, also expires as many unrelated dentries from the cold end of the main LRU, even with the cache far below its memory limit.  import_reverse() counts the same way.

In io500, mdtest-easy-delete leaves millions of null dentries, and at its end the emptied dirfrags of a distributed directory are exported. The trims after these exports pushed every cached dentry of the mdtest-hard directory, which no phase had touched since mdtest-hard-stat, out of the cache of the exporting MDS: on one MDS the cached inodes fell from 1.24M to 118, with the cache at 4.8 GB of its 24 GB limit.  Its mdtest-hard dirfrags, now empty in cache, were then exported back to the MDS of the parent directory, and mdtest-hard-read began by fetching them from RADOS and exporting them out again, stalling for about 20 s.

Count only the dentries that are left in the main LRU.

One host, 3 OSDs on NVMe, 3 active MDS with a distributed tree pin on the mdtest directories, 24 GB MDS cache, 4 kernel client mounts (each a separate kernel client), 16 mdtest processes (4 per client), io500 mdtest phases only, 300 s stonewall, 1 run each:

```
+-----------------------------------+------------+------------+------+
| Phase / count                     | Before     | After      | Diff |
+-----------------------------------+------------+------------+------+
| mdtest-easy-delete (kIOPS)        | 8.94       | 9.97       | +11% |
| mdtest-hard-read (kIOPS)          | 23.67      | 26.19      | +11% |
| Inodes cached on one MDS at the   | 348        | 967083     |      |
| start of mdtest-hard-read         |            |            |      |
+-----------------------------------+------------+------------+------+
```

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81918

72871.title: mgr: do not let a module use a RADOS client before the monitor has it
72871.author: NitzanMordhai
72871.body:
This replaces #51169 . That PR was approved in May 2023 and later closed because it was not active. The problem and the tracker ticket come from @ajarr . In November 2025 he said someone else can take it.

## The problem

  A mgr module opens its own RADOS client and starts to use it right away.
  The address reaches the monitor only with the next beacon. When the
  monitor drops the active mgr, it blocklists `mgrmap.clients`:

  ```cpp
  /* blocklist RADOS clients in use by the mgr */
  for (const auto& a : pending_map.clients) {
    mon.osdmon()->blocklist(a.second, until);
  } 
 ```
  If the client is not in that list yet, the monitor skips it. So after a
  failover the old mgr module can keep writing, because the OSDs still
  accept its requests. At the same time the new mgr runs the same module
  and does the same work. 

  On vstart this gap is 2.2 to 2.8 seconds, every time. The first commit
  adds a selftest command, so the problem is easy to see:
 
  $ ceph mgr self-test rados-client-register
  10.20.192.82:0/829682523
  $ ceph mgr dump | jq .active_clients    # address is missing
  $ ceph mgr fail x 
  $ ceph osd blocklist ls                 # address is missing here too
  The fix

  Registration now blocks until the client is in the MgrMap. The wait is
  woken up from handle_mgr_map(). That function already runs for every
  new map, and it takes the same lock that protects the client set. So we
  do not need epoch numbers and we do not need a polling loop. 

Two commits come before the wait, to make it fast:

  1. The mgr asks for a beacon when the client set changes. Before, it
     waited for the tick.
  2. The monitor proposes at once instead of waiting for
     paxos_propose_interval.
    
| build | register to monitor has it | mgr activate to available |
| --- | --- | --- |
| before | 0.2-1.7s | 1.01-1.13s |
| after | 0.006s | 1.17-1.22s |


  Without the monitor commit, the same wait costs 3.02-3.15s of startup.
Module loads run one after another on a single finisher, so each one
waits for a propose interval.

## What was missing in #51169

`mgr_util` registered the CephFS client *after* `fs.mount()`. But the
mount is the first I/O of that client. So a fix only in C++ does not
help `volumes`, `snap_schedule` and `mirroring`, even if it looks
correct. Now the registration happens between `init()` and `mount()`.
For this, `get_addrs()` needed a small change: it required a mounted
client, but `ceph_getaddrs()` needs only `is_initialized()`.

The second difference is the latency. In #51169 every registration waited
a full beacon period, and nothing made it shorter. This is why the fs,
orch and rados suites failed with ENOTSUP, and why cephadm upgrades hung.

`Mgr::init()` also registers the libcephsqlite client, but it does not
wait. It holds `Mgr::lock`, and after `mgr_module_load_expiration` the
tick thread takes `MgrStandby::lock` and then `Mgr::lock` inside
`exceeded_initialization_expiration()`. Then no beacon can be sent and
the wait never ends. It also does not need to wait, because module loads
are queued after `init()` on the same finisher. In #51169 this was solved
by releasing `Mgr::lock` around the wait and repeating the loop in a
second place.

## Tests

`qa/workunits/mgr/test_client_registration.sh`. I ran it on vstart: it
fails on the commit that adds it, and passes on the next commit.

It needs `mgr_debug_client_register_delay`, a dev option added with the
beacon commit. After the beacon change the gap is only a few
milliseconds, and one `ceph mgr dump` call is slower than that, so the
test cannot see the gap without this option. The existing
`mgr_module_load_delay` option works the same way.

I did not run teuthology yet. The `-ECANCELED` and `-ETIMEDOUT` paths in
`wait_client_registered()` are also not tested.

## Change in behaviour

Registration can fail now. After `mgr_client_register_timeout` (default
30s, 0 means wait forever) the module gets a RuntimeError from
`_ceph_register_client`. Befo

72875.title: .github: label qa/cephfs changes, and flag new QA log ignorelist entries
72875.author: dvanders
72875.body:
The overrides in `qa/cephfs/overrides/` are linked into every fs suite (and into orch/cephadm/nfs, through `fs/nfs`), so a one-line change there reaches much further than the diff suggests. #70177 ran into exactly this: a reasonable fix for a noisy NFS suite that also quieted `MDS_CLIENT_LATE_RELEASE` across all of CephFS QA, which only came to light after it merged (#72636). Nothing in our tooling would have pointed that out to the author or the reviewer, so this PR tries to make it visible up front.

1. **Label `qa/cephfs` changes.** The labeler's `cephfs` rule misses `qa/cephfs/`, so a PR touching only that directory doesn't get the `cephfs` label. The first commit adds `qa/cephfs/**` to it. The matching CODEOWNERS section, which asks the CephFS team to review, is now in #72877, as requested.

2. **Make new ignorelist entries visible.** The second commit adds an optional "QA log ignorelist" section to the PR checklist, and a workflow that fails when a PR adds `log-ignorelist` entries to a qa yaml unless that item is ticked. It lists the new entries per file, compares against the merge base, and skips symlinks, so linking an existing ignorelist into a new suite does not trigger it. Like the config-diff and `.qa` link checks, it runs the script from main and reads the PR only through the API.

Over the 717 merges to main since 2026-08-20, the check would have fired on 17, mostly a team adding entries to its own suite, where ticking the box costs nothing. The aim is just a prompt to loop in the owning team; once #72877 adds CephFS to CODEOWNERS, that team will usually already be on the PR by the time the question comes up.

### Testing
`pull_request_target` workflows run from main, so this one cannot run on this PR. I ran the script locally against real PRs:

| PR | result |
|---|---|
| #70177 | fails, listing `MDS_CLIENT_LATE_RELEASE` and `responding to mclientcaps` in `qa/cephfs/overrides/ignorelist_health.yaml` |
| #70177, box ticked | passes |
| #72636 | passes, no entries added |
| #69320 | its new `ignorelist_*.yaml` symlinks are skipped; its two new task yamls are flagged |
| #68893 | flags its 5 new entries in `qa/overrides/upgrade_ignorelist_health.yaml` |

The template, filled in with the new box ticked, still passes `ceph-pr-checklist-action`, which treats the new section as optional.

72877.title: .github: fill CODEOWNERS gaps
72877.author: dvanders
72877.body:
Follow-up to #72875. Several paths that `.github/labeler.yml` already assigns to a component have no CODEOWNERS entry, so a PR touching only those paths gets the team's label but no review request from that team. The first commit adds the owner the labeler already implies, and nothing else:

| team | added |
|---|---|
| crimson | `qa/suites/crimson-rados` |
| core | the core mgr modules (balancer, crash, devicehealth, insights, localpool, osd_perf_query, osd_support, pg_autoscaler, progress) and the mgr python framework files next to `/src/mgr`; `src/test/{librados,mon,mgr}`; the kvstore, monstore, objectstore, crush, monmap and osdmap tools |
| rbd | the immutable object cache: tool, tests, qa tasks, options, systemd units |
| rgw | `src/cls/timeindex`, `src/test/librgw_*`, the rgw mgr module, `qa/tasks/kafka_failover.py` |
| smb | `qa/tasks/smb.py`, `qa/workunits/smb`, paired with `@ceph/orchestrators` like the other smb entries |

The second commit covers component code that neither file assigns but whose owner is not in doubt:

| team | added |
|---|---|
| orchestrators | `src/ceph-node-proxy`, the ceph_secrets mgr module |
| orchestrators + cephfs | the nfs mgr module, which manages both the NFS service and its CephFS exports |
| core | `src/osdc`, `src/crypto`, `src/compressor`, `src/extblkdev`, `src/test/objectstore`, `qa/objectstore`, `qa/objectstore_debug` |
| crimson | `qa/objectstore_crimson`, `qa/suites/crimson-rados-experimental` |

The third commit asks the release manager to review the release files: `PendingReleaseNotes`, `doc/releases` (with doc-writers), `qa/distros`, `qa/releases` and `src/ceph_release`, and, together with `@ceph/core`, which maintains them, `qa/suites/upgrade` and `qa/overrides/upgrade_ignorelist_health.yaml`, the ignorelist the upgrade suites share.

The fourth commit, moved here from #72875, adds a CephFS section: the paths the labeler maps to cephfs, plus `qa/cephfs` (the overrides shared by every fs suite), the CephFS tests and tools, the mount.ceph helper and the stats module. It sits after core, so `MDSMonitor.*` and `FSCommands.*` ask both `@ceph/core` and `@ceph/cephfs`.

The first commit also drops three entries that match no file: `qa/tasks/mgr/test_cephadm_orchestrator.py` (removed in 2020), `src/spawn` (removed in 2024) and `src/test/cls_otp` (never added).

Each team, please check your own lines; if a path should go elsewhere or be left unowned, say so and I'll adjust.

Two calls I made that may deserve a second look:
- `mgr_module.py`, `mgr_util.py` and the other mgr framework files go to `@ceph/core`, since core owns `/src/mgr`, although every mgr module depends on them.
- The smb qa files are paired with orch, matching the existing smb lines, rather than owned by `@ceph/smb` alone.

### Not in this PR
Some busy paths have no owner and no obvious one: `src/common`, `src/include`, `src/auth`, `src/messages`, the prometheus and telemetry mgr modules, and shared qa plumbing such as the rest of `qa/overrides`, `qa/config` and `qa/clusters`. Those need a decision from the teams rather than a mechanical change.

Two teams named in or relevant to CODEOWNERS lack write access to this repo, so GitHub silently skips them: `@ceph/ceph-csi-maintainers` (already listed for `/doc/csi/`, flagged by GitHub's CODEOWNERS check) and `@ceph/nvmeof`. Fixing that needs an org admin.

### Testing
I resolved every tracked file against the new CODEOWNERS with git's wildmatch rules. Every file the labeler maps to crimson, core, rbd, rgw, smb, mon or mgr now has an owner, and no rule is left matching nothing. This PR gives an owner to 2,495 files (885 from the first three commits, 1,610 from the CephFS section); unowned files on main drop from 5,441 to 2,946 (of 14,985).

72878.title: rgw: reject zero-stripe implicit manifest rules (fix IBMCEPH-20552)
72878.author: chardan
72878.body:
Fixes IBMCEPH-20552

Implicit object manifests with zero stripe capacity can stall iteration or cause division by zero in the generator. Reject every zero-capacity implicit rule independently of decoded object/head sizes, including rules hidden by apparent empty or head-only layouts. Preserve default empty manifests and valid head-only, multipart and explicit layouts.

72879.title: [RFC] osd: write journal for optimized EC pools (DNM)
72879.author: vitaly-goot
72879.body:
## Summary

This PR introduces a proof-of-concept write journal for optimized erasure-coded pools. The design, measurements, sizing and open questions are in the RFC document [doc/dev/ec-write-journal-poc.rst](https://github.com/vitaly-goot/ceph/blob/vgoot/osd/ec-write-journal/doc/dev/ec-write-journal-poc.rst), part of this PR.

Small aligned overwrites currently require a full read-modify-write cycle, serialize through the PG pipeline, and generate PG log and RocksDB metadata updates on every touched shard. The journal instead:

- appends eligible writes to replicated PG-local journal slots;
- acknowledges the client after all `m + 1` journal holders commit the record;
- coalesces journaled updates into later standard EC stripe writes;
- serves reads by overlaying live journal data on data read from the EC shards; and
- reconstructs journal state from slot metadata after peering or primary changes.

The feature is experimental, disabled by default, and restricted to one explicitly enrolled EC pool. It was developed and measured as a prototype on v20.2.4 (tentacle) and then ported to `main`; the `main` port has been compile-checked and unit-tested but not yet run on a cluster.

## Implementation

- Add the EC journal record format, in-memory index, slot lifecycle, and replay logic.
- Replicate journal records on shard 0 and the parity shards, preserving tolerance of up to `m` failures.
- Add a flush planner that:
  - coalesces updates to the same stripe;
  - avoids chunk reads when journal records cover a complete stripe;
  - recycles slots once their records are superseded or materialized; and
  - emits ordinary logged EC writes for final materialization.
- Support:
  - client reads over journaled data;
  - writes crossing one stripe boundary;
  - request replay and duplicate replies;
  - `user_version` and `mtime` overlays;
  - direct-write absorption of overlapping journaled stripes;
  - PG split handling; and
  - controlled draining and graceful shutdown.
- Carry the prerequisite fixes for optimized EC peering with partial writes (PRs #72228 and #72260, open separately) and two generic fast-EC fixes: completed client reads leave the in-flight list before their callbacks run, and log entries list every shard while the PG is degraded or undersized.
- Defer roll-forward kicks for the enrolled pool to avoid unnecessary metadata transactions between writes.
- Add PG-query observability for journal capacity, records, segments, admission decisions, flushes, replay state, and duplicate-request tracking.

## Configuration

The journal is controlled by the following options:

- `osd_ec_journal_enable` — globally enables the experimental feature.
- `osd_ec_journal_pool` — selects the single enrolled pool.
- `osd_ec_journal_max_bytes` — journal budget per PG; defaults to 64 MiB.
- `osd_ec_journal_max_flushes` — maximum concurrent stripe flushes per PG.
- `osd_ec_journal_max_write_bytes` — maximum eligible write size; defaults to 32 KiB.
- `osd_ec_journal_drain` — stops admission, flushes all records, and removes slot objects.
- `osd_ec_rollforward_delay_ms` — delays roll-forward kicks for the enrolled pool.

Eligible pools are currently limited to optimized 4+3, 8+3, or 12+3 EC profiles with 4 KiB chunks.

## Prototype results

All cluster results below come from the v20.2.4 prototype; the `main` port is compile-checked and unit-tested only, and cluster testing on `main` is pending. Testing on an 11-node, 55-NVMe OSD cluster using an 8+3 EC profile showed:

- up to **1.9x write IOPS** for hot 4 KiB random writes;
- approximately **1.3x-1.5x write IOPS** for mixed write sizes;
- **20%-54% lower total block-device writes** with a 256 MiB journal budget; and
- no measurable regression for unenrolled pools: within 1% IOPS p99 latency of the unmodified v20.2.4 baseline.

Throughput converges toward baseline (ec-fast) for cold workloads where writes rarely coalesce. With the default 64 MiB budget, the coldest tested workloads were slightly

72884.title: os/bluestore: add bluestore_page_cache_read
72884.author: dvanders
72884.body:
BlueStore opens the block device O_DIRECT, so object data is cached only by
BlueStore itself, inside `osd_memory_target`. Running small OSDs means a small
target, and the data cache shrinks with it.

This adds `bluestore_page_cache_read` (default off). Object data reads then go
through the buffered descriptor, so the kernel page cache can act as the data
cache. It is sized by memory the host isn't otherwise using and given back under
pressure. This is what `bluefs_buffered_io` already does for RocksDB reads,
extended to object data.

### How it works
- `blk`: `aio_read()` gains a `buffered` flag (default false). A buffered read
  is a synchronous `pread()` on the buffered fd: libaio would block at submit on
  a non-O_DIRECT fd. io_uring is not used.
- `os/bluestore`: only blobs **with a checksum** are read through the page
  cache. A stale page, for example after a racing O_DIRECT write, then fails
  verification instead of being returned. When a page-cache read fails its
  checksum, the cached pages are dropped and the read is retried O_DIRECT;
  retries never use the page cache. Reads hinted NOCACHE/DONTNEED stay O_DIRECT.
- New perf counters: `page_cache_read_bytes`, `page_cache_csum_retries`.
- To avoid caching data twice, shrink BlueStore's own data cache when enabling
  this, e.g. `bluestore_cache_meta_ratio=0.5`, `bluestore_cache_kv_ratio=0.45`,
  `bluestore_cache_kv_onode_ratio=0.04`.

### Measurements
vstart with 6 OSDs, 256 PGs/OSD, an rbd pool at size 3 with a 24 GiB image
(72 GiB of replicas), `bluestore_debug_enforce_settings=hdd`, local NVMe. All
OSDs ran in one cgroup with a hard `memory.max` that also counts the page
cache. Phases: sequential fill, 3 GiB of 4K random writes, two passes of 4K
random reads, osd.0 out/in recovery, deep scrub.

| osd_memory_target / cgroup cap per OSD | 4K randread / re-read ops/s, off → on |
|---|---|
| 1.5 GiB / 2 GiB | 31,207 / 31,523 → 33,313 / 33,974 (+7% / +8%) |
| 1 GiB / 1 GiB (*) | 30,436 / 30,601 → 32,870 / 33,823 (+8% / +11%) |

(*) With a shorter PG log and smaller RocksDB memtables; at defaults, a 1 GiB
target OOMs on this workload whether or not this option is enabled.

- The page cache filled whatever the cap left free, and the kernel reclaimed it
  at the limit with no OOM kills.
- Random writes and per-OSD RSS were unchanged.
- **0 checksum retries** in about 125 GiB read through the page cache across
  all runs.

### Resolved: memory left after recovery
In 2 of 3 runs with this option and the low data-cache ratios together, the OSD that was marked out and back in ended recovery with ~80 MiB in the `bluestore_writing` mempool. This was not caused by this change. The OSD op history kept the last 20 recovery pushes and their data, because `MOSDPGPush` did not drop its buffers once an op was done. It reproduces with this option off, on a 3-OSD cluster with default settings. Fixed separately in #72885 (tracker 81945).

72885.title: messages/MOSDPGPush: drop push buffers once the op is done
72885.author: dvanders
72885.body:
A finished op stays in the OSD's op history (`osd_op_history_size`, 20 ops, for up to `osd_op_history_duration`, 600 s), and `OpRequest::_unregistered()` calls `Message::clear_data()` so that the history keeps the description, not the data. `MOSDOp` and `MOSDECSubOpWrite` drop their decoded buffers in `clear_buffers()`; `MOSDPGPush` did not, so every push in the history kept the object data it carried, up to `osd_recovery_max_chunk`.

Clearing `PushOp::data` alone is not enough: the xattrs in `attrset` are decoded as slices of the same receive buffer as the data, so even a small attribute keeps the whole push alive. This drops data, omap and attrset.

After recovery the history is typically all pushes, so an idle OSD held 20 × 4 MiB of rbd object data. It shows up in the `bluestore_writing` mempool, because BlueStore tagged the buffers when it wrote them.

### Reproducer
vstart, 3 OSDs, pool size 3: stop osd.0, write 30 × 4 MiB objects with `rados put`, start osd.0, wait for active+clean.

| | `dump_historic_ops` | `bluestore_writing` on osd.0 |
|---|---|---|
| before | 20 × MOSDPGPush | 20 items, 80 MiB |
| with this change | 20 × MOSDPGPush | 0 bytes |

Without the change, setting `osd_op_history_size` to 0 frees it too.

Found while measuring OSD memory for #72884. `MOSDECSubOpReadReply` (`buffers_read`) may have the same issue on EC pools; not tested here.

72886.title: mon/MonClient: reopen session if active_con never becomes ready
72886.author: yzhan298
72886.body:
When two monitors are stopped at almost the same time, a MonClient whose session was on the first one can re-hunt and authenticate with the second one just before it exits. The client then keeps a dead session forever: hunting has finished, every message to the mon is lost, and nothing recovers until that same monitor comes back.

Proposed fix:

MonClient::tick(): if active_con's connection has not been connected (is_connected() is false, i.e. msgr2 not READY) for longer than mon_client_ping_timeout, call _reopen_session(). This does not depend on peer features. A new session then triggers OSD::ms_handle_connect() -> send_alive().

Plus a dev-only injection, ms_inject_stall_server_ident: the server does not reply to CLIENT_IDENT from non-mon peers. This lets a qa/standalone test reproduce the zombie session deterministically:
3 mons; freeze mon.b; turn on the injection on mon.c
start a client that knows only mon.b and mon.c, so it can only land on mon.c
kill mon.c, unfreeze mon.b
the client must get a session within 120s
Without the fix the client is stuck until client_mount_timeout; with the fix it re-hunts after mon_client_ping_timeout.

tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81947

72887.title: script/ptl-tool: summarize unsent kernel testing commits in QA tracker
72887.author: vshankar
72887.body:
Add --kernel-commits which, when creating or updating a QA tracker, summarizes the commits in the ceph-client "testing" branch that have not yet been sent to Linus, i.e. for-linus..testing. The section links to the pinned testing sha1 and a GitHub compare view, and counts the commits per subject prefix rather than listing each one, since testing can carry 100+ commits.

The fs suite runs kclient jobs against the testing kernel, so knowing which kernel driver changes were under test helps when verifying a run: failures can be checked against those commits to tell whether they may have been caused by the kernel driver rather than by the PRs in the branch.

The data is fetched via the GitHub API, so no local kernel clone is needed. The repo and branch names can be overridden with PTL_TOOL_KERNEL_REPO, PTL_TOOL_KERNEL_TESTING_BRANCH and PTL_TOOL_KERNEL_FOR_LINUS_BRANCH.

In --dry-run mode, also log the QA tracker description as readable text so the generated section can be reviewed.

**Description**

Currently, ceph_rgw_metadata does not expose the RGW zone ID, making it difficult to correlate RGW daemon-level metrics with the bucket and user usage metrics exported through Prometheus Pushgateway.

72895.title: mds: join the metrics updater without holding mds_lock
72895.author: LiShengG
72895.body:
MDSRankDispatcher::shutdown() calls MetricsHandler::shutdown() with mds_lock held, and that joins the mds-metrics updater thread. The updater does not re-check MetricsHandler::stopping after it wakes from its sleep, and update_rank0() reads subvolume rbytes through MDSRank::get_inode_rbytes(), which takes mds_lock. If a client reported subvolume metrics in the last update interval, the updater blocks on mds_lock held by the thread joining it, and the MDS hangs on SIGTERM.

Re-checking MetricsHandler::stopping in the updater would not be enough: update_rank0() drops the metrics lock before it calls get_inode_rbytes(), so shutdown can set it and join right then. Instead, drop mds_lock around the join, the same way shutdown() waits for the rank finisher to stop. MDSRank::stopping is already set by then. get_inode_rbytes() does not check it, but it only reads the projected rstat of a cached inode, and the cache is not torn down until later, so the updater can finish that read while the rank shuts down.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81946

72900.title: client, mds: fix slow creates, stats and unlinks in directories spread over several MDSs
72900.author: xiubli
72900.body:
`ceph-fuse` and `libcephfs` clients working together in a directory whose fragments are spread over several active MDSs, as `ceph.dir.pin.distributed` does, crawl: with 8 ceph-fuse ranks `mdtest-hard-delete` ran at 0.21 kIOPS instead of 1.60 with the directory on one MDS. Three fixes:

- **client: do not ask for Fs on a directory in ll_lookup()**: a cached directory was only used when Fs was issued, which never happens while its filelock is in MIX, so every revalidation moved the filelock MIX -> SYNC on the auth (47 times a second), gathering it from the other MDSs.
- **client: check caps after a cap import**: a cap update dropped during an export left the client holding Fx/Fw/Fb on files it had closed, and every stat from another client had to revoke them.
- **mds: flush the journal when a cap update holds up a filelock change**: a cap update answering a revoke waited for the next periodic journal flush, up to 5 s per file.

Plus a qa job, fs/multiclient `shared-dir-unlink`: all clients create and then remove files in one directory under `ceph.dir.pin.distributed` with 2 active MDSs, and the job fails when either phase takes longer than 10 minutes.

Split out of #72265 at review (@dvanders). That PR's `ceph.dir.pin.distributed.tree` spreads many directories this way, so clients need these fixes for it.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81952

## Testing

- Each commit builds on its own on main (ceph-mds, ceph-fuse), no new warnings.
- The new job run locally (vstart, 2 active MDSs, 3 ceph-fuse mounts for the 3 clients of fs/multiclient, 4 processes and 80k files each, in one directory under ceph.dir.pin.distributed), per client:

  | phase | this branch | without "client: do not ask for Fs on a directory in ll_lookup()" |
  |---|---|---|
  | create | ~700/s, 110-115 s | ~40/s, ~2000 s |
  | unlink | ~600/s, 125-140 s | killed by the 10 min timeout |

- With 12 mdtest ranks on 3 ceph-fuse mounts and 240k files in one directory spread by ceph.dir.pin.distributed.tree (with #72265): 3123 removes/s; without the ll_lookup() commit the run did not finish in 20 minutes, and at 24k files it removed 352 files/s against 4245.
- The io500 numbers in the commit messages were measured with #72265 applied, on 4 ceph-fuse client nodes.

This PR logs the missing information before teardown destroys it:

72910.title: mon/AuthMonitor: check entity health incrementally
72910.author: polyedre
72910.body:
Every auth write seems to get slower as a cluster gains auth entities. We are testing one cephx identity per (volume, hypervisor), so tens of thousands of entities, and there a single `auth get-or-create` takes more than half a second, and concurrent writes drop to about one per second.

I think it comes from `AuthMonitor::check_health()`: it runs on every auth proposal and parses the caps and checks the key type of every entity, under the monitor lock.

- The first commit keeps the health verdicts of the committed entities that have something to report, and updates them from the incrementals `update_from_paxos()` applies. They are rebuilt after a full load, a reset, or a change of `mon_auth_validate_all_caps`. A pending incremental now replaces the verdict of its entity instead of adding to it, so the health stored with a proposal matches the entities of that proposal.
- The second commit bounds the detail of `AUTH_BAD_CAPS` and `AUTH_INSECURE_*_KEY_TYPE` to `mon_health_max_detail` entities, as PG health checks do. The whole health map is stored with every proposal, and on a cluster where clients still have `aes` keys, every client entity was listed on each auth write. The summary still counts them all.

With both commits backported to 20.2.4, a get-or-create with 35,000 entities went back to about the cost of an empty cluster, and concurrent writes were roughly 10 times faster. `qa/standalone/mon/auth-health.sh` covers bad caps raised, fixed and removed, a leader failover, a monitor restart, the option toggle, and the detail bound.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81958

72911.title: mgr/cephadm: don't mute auth health warnings on clusters with auth_allowed_ciphers if already aes256k-only
72911.author: ShwetaBhosale1

Fixes:

72912.title: osd/PeeringState: stamp last_clean in pg_stat_t, not pg_history_t
72912.author: shraddhaag
72912.body:
## Issue

We see a performance regression with the PR https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/72144. For small (4K) random writes, we see a significant IOPS regression in crimson: 

| OSD | Block size | Before | Regression | Fix |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | Crimson + SeaStore | 4k | 37,776 | 6,349 (−83.2%) | 38,199 (+1.1%) |
  | Crimson + SeaStore | 1M | 2,256 | 2,249 (−0.3%) | 2,291 (+1.6%) |
  | Classic + BlueStore | 4k | 54,929 | 53,190 (−3.2%) | 54,231 (−1.3%) |
  | Classic + BlueStore | 1M | 2,755 | 2,756 (+0.0%) | 2,756 (+0.0%) |

Setup: 1 OSD on NVMe (LVM volume), fio rbd engine, randwrite, 8 jobs x iodepth 32, 60 s per run, crimson with `--crimson-smp 4`. The 1M results are limited by the NVMe device.

Commits: before [`91514feb517`](https://github.com/ceph/ceph/commit/91514feb517e829db3d7639f58f55753323fccb6), regression [`ff2f4a0d988`](https://github.com/ceph/ceph/commit/ff2f4a0d988c7377e27f2c20f57caf87da4dcf78), fix [`fa3d949306f`](https://github.com/shraddhaag/ceph/commit/fa3d949306f3b5973fbee97f34657b2bb772cdb5)([`ff2f4a0d988`](https://github.com/ceph/ceph/commit/ff2f4a0d988c7377e27f2c20f57caf87da4dcf78) + fix).

## Root Cause 

Primary OSD updates `last_clean` on each write. PR https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/72144 moved the `last_clean` field from `pg_stat_t` into `pg_history_t`. 

`_fastinfo` only tracks a subset of fields in `_info`. An update in `pg_stat_t` is covered by `_fastinfo` but an update in `pg_history_t` is not. Since each write updates `last_clean` in `pg_history_t`, `_fastinfo` will in almost all cases will not suffice. We will almost always have to do a complete `_info` update. 

A `_fastinfo` update is  about 194 bytes, while an `_info` save is about 1110 bytes. On each write op we are writing about 900 bytes more. 

I verified the `_fastinfo` share of PG info saves: 

  | OSD | Before | Regression | Fix |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Crimson + SeaStore | 99.7% | 0% | 99.7% |
  | Classic + BlueStore | 99.0% | 21.7% | 99.0% |

## Impact on Classic

RocksDB appends the pg log entry and the info update. Now instead of `_fastinfo` it appends `_info`. The difference is 900 bytes on each write. Since its an append we do not see a huge performance regression. 

## Impact on Crimson 

When Seastore needs to save a `_fastinfo`, it generally overwrites over the previous `_fastinfo` entry. But when it needs to save the `_info`, it needs to find the old `_info`, mark it removed and then append the new `_info`. The chain traversal to find the old `_info` is the extra work that seastore does on each write and hence leads to a large performance impact. 

## Fix 

Move the `last_clean` field back in `pg_stat_t`. 

When a vulnerability window closes (the first clean publish after the onset), we set `pg_history_t.vuln_window_reported` and `pg_history_t.last_clean` to the current time. We do not read `pg_stat_t.last_clean`, because peering copies `pg_stat_t` from other OSDs.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81977

72916.title: crimson/osd: spread primary PGs evenly across cores
72916.author: Matan-B
72916.body:
New PGs were assigned based only on total PG count, which could lead to primaries accumulating on a subset of cores.
Since primary PGs handle client write execution, replication operations, and responses, this created noticeable load imbalance. In a 4K randwrite workload with 4 reactors, the busiest cores handled roughly 1.6× more primary writes than the least busy ones.

With this PR, PGs for which the OSD is primary are placed on the core with the fewest primary PG, while other PGs continue to follow the existing placement policy.

Per-core primary counts are also kept up to date as PG roles change, ensuring new PG placements are made using the current primary distribution.

This provides a more even spread of primary workload across reactors and helps reduce core hotspots without moving already mapped PGs between cores.

72917.title: doc/cephadm: fix the OSD, host management and operations pages
72917.author: eameh-LF
72917.body:
A follow-up to #72731, #72733 and #72734, with corrections to three cephadm pages: OSD Service, Host Management and Cephadm Operations. Each page keeps its sections and their order, and no label or section link breaks.

What changed:

- OSD sizes: the exact `size` example is now `3.64T`, written as `ceph-volume` reports the size. `10T` matched no 10 TB drive. The page also says that a range takes only whole numbers: `9.1T:15T` is accepted, but no OSDs are created from it.
- OSD page: the `libstoragemgmt` warning now comes before the command that turns on the enhanced device scan. The `ceph-volume inventory` example under Filters runs in `cephadm shell`, and the HDD model in two hardware lists and one spec is `HDD-123-foo`, not `SSD-123-foo`.
- Host management: the `ceph orch host maintenance exit` synopsis and text now show that `--offline` needs `--force`. The Sudo Hardening section now has a label, so that the operations page can link to it.
- Operations: the key rotation section now names `ceph orch rotate-key` as well as `ceph orch daemon rotate-key`, and says that in releases before Squid 19.2.6 and Tentacle 20.2.4 these commands can take daemons such as NFS and NVMe-oF down. The page also says that cephadm refuses to stop the whole `mgr`, `mon` or `osd` service.
- Operations: the page now says that `cluster-start` starts the admin host first, and waits up to five minutes for the placement groups to become `active+clean`. The keyring list names both copies of the keyring, and the journald note gives the Podman version, 2.1.0.

The commit messages list each correction.

Preview: https://ceph--72917.org.readthedocs.build/en/72917/cephadm/services/osd/, https://ceph--72917.org.readthedocs.build/en/72917/cephadm/host-management/ and https://ceph--72917.org.readthedocs.build/en/72917/cephadm/operations/

Review notes:

- This PR adds no conflict to any open PR that changes these pages.
- Not in this PR: the TPM2 sentence on the OSD page should say that support starts with Squid 19.2.1. A fix here would conflict with #72680, which adds text right above it.
- For the page owner: `ceph orch apply` accepts a size range with a decimal, such as `9.1T:15T`, and the spec fails only later, with `CEPHADM_APPLY_SPEC_FAIL`. Should the command reject it instead?
- Checked against the source. Nothing was run on a cluster. Strict build adds no warning to those already on main.

72918.title: doc/cephadm: fix the monitoring, gateway, OAuth2 proxy and certificate pages
72918.author: eameh-LF
72918.body:
A follow-up to #72736 and #72737, with corrections to four cephadm pages: Monitoring Services, Management Gateway, OAuth2 Proxy and Certificate Management. Each page keeps its sections and their order, and no label or section link breaks.

What changed:

- Monitoring setup: bootstrap deploys `ceph-exporter` on every host, but the setup steps left it out. By default, a cluster set up with them had no daemon performance counters in Prometheus. The page now names `ceph-exporter` in the stack, deploys it in the first step and removes it with the other services. The `ceph orch ls` paragraph now follows the deploy steps, not the Grafana URL command.
- Monitoring reference: the custom image options now include `container_image_alloy`, for Umbrella 21 and later releases, and the lists of file templates name `services/alloy` and `services/alloy.j2`. The page now says that only the active Manager serves metrics, and that standby Managers listen on the same port but return none. The mailing list URL under Default Images is now a link.
- Gateway: the credentials link now opens Enabling Security for the Monitoring Stack, not the top of Monitoring Services. It uses a new label on that section. The Prometheus module page already used that label, so its link works too, and the strict build has one warning fewer. The cipher warning no longer says "at this moment".
- OAuth2 proxy: the page now says that the login covers access through the gateway only. By default, Grafana still allows anonymous read-only access on its own port. `ceph orch apply mgmt-gateway` is now a step only for a cluster without a gateway, as it replaces an existing gateway specification with the defaults. The page also says that cephadm does not turn Dashboard SSO back on, and that `ceph dashboard sso enable oauth2` is refused until an `oauth2-proxy` daemon is running.
- Certificates: the health check section no longer contradicts itself. It now says that cephadm raises no health check for cephadm-signed certificates while automated rotation is on, and only a warning for a user-provided certificate near expiry. The page also says that a spec with only one of `ssl_cert` and `ssl_key` is rejected, and the notes under `cert rm` and `key rm` are now note boxes.

The commit messages list each correction.

Preview: https://ceph--72918.org.readthedocs.build/en/72918/cephadm/services/monitoring/, https://ceph--72918.org.readthedocs.build/en/72918/cephadm/services/mgmt-gateway/, https://ceph--72918.org.readthedocs.build/en/72918/cephadm/services/oauth2-proxy/ and https://ceph--72918.org.readthedocs.build/en/72918/cephadm/certmgr/

Review notes:

To keep clear of #72672, which adds Pushgateway entries close to the Promtail ones, the Alloy image option follows the Loki one, and the Alloy templates follow the Alertmanager ones.
- My draft #72863 rewrites the same link on the Prometheus module page, because the label was missing. If this PR merges first, that change is no longer needed.
- Not in this PR: the Dashboard page gives `ceph orch apply mgmt-gateway --enable_auth=true --placement=<ceph-node-02>` as a step for single sign-on. That command replaces the gateway specification too, so the page needs a change of its own.

72943.title: neorados: drop unused cls_lock_client link
72943.author: djgalloway
72943.body:
Since #68593 (osd: include cleanup) merged on 2026-10-16, every ceph-dev-pipeline **noble / x86_64 / debug** build has failed to link `bin/neorados`:

```
undefined reference to `librados::v14_2_0::ObjectOperation::ObjectOperation()'
undefined reference to `librados::v14_2_0::IoCtx::operate(...)'
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status
make[3]: *** [src/tools/CMakeFiles/neorados.dir/build.make:133: bin/neorados] Error 1
```

This happens on main and on every branch based on it. Example: https://jenkins.ceph.com/job/ceph-dev-pipeline/10059/ (main: #9949 onward; last good was #9929 at a4692027).

### Cause

`libneorados` links `cls_lock_client`, but nothing in neorados uses it. In a Debug build (`-Og`) with Ubuntu's default `-flto=auto -ffat-lto-objects`, Boost program_options needs `std::string::operator[]`. The linker takes it from a weak copy in `cls_lock_client.cc.o`, and the rest of that object needs librados, which `bin/neorados` does not link.

### Fix

- Drop `cls_lock_client` from `libneorados`.
- Link `cls_lock_client` directly into `ceph_test_librbd` and `ceph_test_rbd_mirror`. They were the only targets getting it through libneorados, and they need it for `rbd_internal`'s `rados::cls::lock` calls. This matches how they already link `cls_rbd_client` and `cls_journal_client`, and how the other targets that link `rbd_internal` (`librbd`, `rbd-mirror`, `unittest_librbd`, `unittest_rbd_mirror`) already link `cls_lock_client`.

Credit to @mmgaggle (Kyle Bader), who diagnosed this and carried the fix as CI-only commits on his `wip-kbader-s3rdma-*` branches ([e9fddc02](https://github.com/ceph/ceph-ci/commit/e9fddc02c2f110f959e3de46b01364891db902f3), [c88dbd7d](https://github.com/ceph/ceph-ci/commit/c88dbd7d8f44fb4269ba88928344383950a858ee)). With those commits, the full matrix passes, noble debug included (ceph-dev-pipeline #10053, #10054, #10069). His version linked `cls_lock_client` into `rbd_internal` instead. Following review, it now goes on the two test targets, so `rbd_internal` is unchanged.

72945.title: rgw: guard a delete's head removal on the ID tag it read
72945.author: AliMasarweh
72945.body:
Continuation to PR https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/72100


55f5b762c67 ("fix conditional Delete and MultiDelete") replaced the delete's call to prepare_atomic_modification(removal_op=true), which added a cmpxattr on the ID tag, with check_preconditions, which adds nothing to the op. A delete that races an overwrite now removes the new head, then sends the manifest it read, the old one, to GC. The new object's tail, or a completion's parts, is never collected.

Guard the removal with append_atomic_test again. DeleteObject already answers the lost race's -ECANCELED with success; answer it the same way in multi-object delete, which reported it as an error before 55f5b762c67 as well.

The workunit case test_delete_racing_put in https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/72096 fails on main (the PutObject's tail remains after GC) and passes with this change on a vstart cluster.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80898

With the removal guarded, a delete can lose the race to a write that replaced the head. DeleteObject answers that with success, which is right for an unconditional delete. A conditional one (If-Match, If-Match-Size, If-Match-Last-Modified-Time, If-Unmodified-Since) cannot claim its condition held, so the second commit answers its lost race with 409 ConditionalRequestConflict, in DeleteObject and in multi-object delete, and adds that error (https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80906). The guard also closes a conditional delete deleting an object that fails its If-Match; the workunit case test_cond_delete_racing_put in https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/72096 fails on main and passes with this change.

Versioned buckets
In a bucket whose versioning is suspended, a DeleteObject of the null version logs the removal of the null instance, and whoever applies the olh log removes its head. If a PutObject wrote the key's head and linked a new null version in between, that removal took the new version's head: the version stayed current and lost its data. A new commit makes apply_olh_log cancel a pending removal when a later entry links the same instance as a version, with "null" and the empty instance treated as the same key.

Validated on vstart with the injection points of https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/72096: the workunit case test_suspended_delete_null_racing_put fails without the new commit and passes with it.

Not covered here:

when the guarded removal inside apply_olh_log loses a race, the error is treated as a race with another applier, and the rewritten head stays until the log is applied again;
a conditional DeleteObject with versionId=null checks its condition apart from the unlink, which needs a cls condition on unlink_instance, like the one https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/72118 adds to link_olh.

72952.title: rgw/multisite: sync compressed objects without recompressing them
72952.author: kchheda3
72952.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81733

Today data sync decompresses a compressed object on the source and the destination
recompresses it with its own settings. When both zones use the same compression type,
that wastes CPU on both sides and sends the uncompressed size over the network. With
this change the object is sent as stored when it already uses the type the destination
would pick. Replicas still follow the destination zone's compression settings.

How it works:
- The destination adds `rgwx-skip-decompress=<class>:<type>,...` to the sync GET. It
  doesn't know the object's storage class until the response arrives, while the source
  does, so it sends the type of every storage class in the destination bucket's placement
  target that has a fixed type, and the source looks up the object's class. `:<type>`
  covers objects without a storage class (the bucket's default class). When a sync policy
  pins the destination class, the object's class doesn't matter, so only `*:<type>` is sent.
- The source sends the object as stored, with `Rgwx-Decompress-Skipped: true`, only if
  the object's class and type match an entry and the request has no Range or partNumber.
  Otherwise it decompresses as before.
- The destination keeps the compression attr and checks it, along with the received
  length. If the class the destination finally resolves uses a different type, it fails
  with an internal error, and sync fetches that object again decompressed.
- Encrypted objects are unchanged (already sent as stored).

Compatibility: an older source ignores the param, so the destination recompresses as
today; an older destination never sends it. `rgw_sync_obj_skip_decompress` (default true)
turns it off. `rgw_sync_obj_etag_verify` doesn't verify objects sent compressed, as with
encrypted objects.

Depends on #72608 and #72508; only the last three commits are new.

72958.title: qa/tasks/mgr/dashboard: write non-zero data in test_copy
72958.author: djgalloway
72958.body:
`tasks.mgr.dashboard.test_rbd.RbdTest.test_copy` fails intermittently in the dashboard API tests ([tracker #68544](https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/68544), open since 2024-10; most recently on [ceph-pr-pipeline 5952](https://jenkins.ceph.com/job/ceph-pr-pipeline/5952/)) with:

```
  File "/ceph/qa/tasks/mgr/dashboard/test_rbd.py", line 791, in test_copy
    self._validate_image(img_copy, ... disk_usage=img['disk_usage'])
AssertionError: 0 != 67108864
```

**Cause:** the test fills the source image with `rbd bench --io-type write --io-total 5M`, and rbd bench's default `--pattern-byte rand` fills its single write buffer with one byte, `memset(bp.c_str(), rand() & 0xff, io_size)` (`src/tools/rbd/action/Bench.cc`, seeded from `time()`). So in about 1 run of 256 every byte written is `0x00`. The source still accounts the written objects (64 MiB), but librbd's copy skips all-zero extents (`if (m_bl->is_zero()) ... return;` in `src/librbd/internal.cc`), so the copy is correctly sparse and reports `disk_usage` 0.

This is not a timing race, so waiting for the copy's usage to converge (#68904, auto-closed unreviewed) would only turn the failure into a `TestTimeoutError` 30 s later.

**Fix:** `--pattern-byte 1`, so the data is never all zeros. The other `rbd bench` calls in `test_rbd.py` (`test_disk_usage`, the rollback test) only check the image they wrote to, which accounts zero-filled writes too, so they're unaffected.

**Backports:** `--pattern-byte` (13a59272967) is on tentacle and umbrella, so this applies there as-is. squid doesn't have it and has the same 1-in-256 behaviour, so a squid backport would need another way to write non-zero data.

72962.title: crimson/net: read the IOHandler shard without touching shard_states
72962.author: tchaikov
72962.body:
The IOHandler is not sharded: each connection has a single instance, shared by the messenger core, its I/O core and every core that sends to it. `send()` and `send_keepalive()` can run on any of them, and they look up the connection's shard with `get_shard_id()`, which goes through the `shard_states` pointer. Only the I/O core is supposed to touch `shard_states`, and it swaps the pointer in `to_new_sid()` and `set_accepted_sid()`, so a sender on another core can find it null or already freed.

The osd.1 log of the failed thrash job shows exactly that: shard 0 accepts a connection from osd.2 and hands it to core 1 with `dispatch_accept(1)`. While core 1 is in `to_new_sid()`, shard 0 gets the same connection back from `send_to_osd()` ("connect to existing"), sends to it, and crashes in `IOHandler::send()`.

So keep the shard id in an atomic, and let `get_shard_id()` read that instead. Senders already recheck the shard after `submit_to()`, so a stale id is fine. In `to_new_sid()`, the new id is set after `io_crosscore.reset_wait()`, since senders on the new core start using `io_crosscore` as soon as they see it.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/75658

72964.title: osd: scale uncached memory limits with a small osd_memory_target
72964.author: dvanders
72964.body:
Follow-up to the review of #72884: rather than adding a second cache, this makes small `osd_memory_target` values work by shrinking what the cache autotuner can't.

The autotuner keeps an OSD near its target by shrinking its caches, but several other consumers are bounded by limits sized for the default 4 GiB, and nothing shrinks them: the RocksDB WAL (and with it the memtables, `max_total_wal_size` = 1 GiB), in-flight client message bytes (`osd_client_message_size_cap` = 500 MiB) and the PG log (300k entries per OSD, 3000 dups per PG). At a 1 GiB target, the caches go to their floor and these still outgrow the budget: under a 1 GiB-per-OSD cgroup limit, OSDs were OOM-killed during 4K random reads, with the PG log alone at 188 MiB.

Below 4 GiB, those limits are multiplied by `osd_memory_target / 4 GiB` while they are at their defaults (the WAL by its square root, which keeps write tail latency unchanged). A value set explicitly is used as is, so operators who already tuned a limit get exactly what they set. At or above 4 GiB nothing changes.

### Results
vstart, 6 OSDs at 256 PGs each, rbd pool at size 3, fio rbd engine, three runs per configuration, caches dropped before each read test:

| | 1 GiB, this PR | 1 GiB, without it | 4 GiB (default) |
|---|---|---|---|
| peak RSS per OSD | **986 MiB** | 1330 MiB | 2097 MiB |
| 4M write, 64 in flight | 752 MiB/s | 760 MiB/s | 763 MiB/s |
| 4K random write | 6884 IOPS | 6787 IOPS | 6817 IOPS |
| ↳ p99 / p99.9 | 8.9 / 16.6 ms | 8.9 / 16.9 ms | 8.9 / 16.9 ms |
| 4K random read, cold | 38276 IOPS | 37513 IOPS | 37773 IOPS |
| 4K read, 3 GiB hot set, warm | 38881 IOPS | 38613 IOPS | 53955 IOPS |
| recovery (one OSD out, in) | 389 s | 392 s | 394 s |

So a 1 GiB OSD stays under 1 GiB at no measurable cost against the same target without this change. The remaining difference to 4 GiB is the hot-set read, which comes from the data cache (onode hit rate was 100% in both); that's what #72884 and @ming1's elastic-target idea are about, and it's out of scope here.

Linear WAL scaling (256 MiB at 1 GiB) cut peak RSS to 794 MiB but raised 4K random write p99.9 latency by 25% (20.7 vs 16.9 ms), from more frequent memtable flushes; hence the square root.

72965.title: cephadm: bind host rootfs with rslave propagation
72965.author: vshankar
72965.body:
OSD and node-exporter containers recursively bind mount the host's / at /rootfs using the default (rprivate) propagation. Every mount that exists on the host when such a container starts gets copied into the container's mount namespace and host umounts never propagatex to it.

`fusermount -u` detaches the host's copy, but the fuse connection stays alive until the container stops, so ceph-fuse never sees the unmount and never exits. This is hit in fs:upgrade suites where the upgrade redeploys OSDs and node-exporter after ceph-fuse has mounted.

Manual debugging (scanning /proc/*/mountinfo for the fuse device right after fusermount -u) confirmed this: the mount was gone from the host mount table but the fuse connection was still alive, and the mount namespaces of the redeployed osd.{0,1,2} and node-exporter containers still held the ceph-fuse mount at /rootfs/<mntpt> with private propagation.

  mnt:[4026533286] pid=101758 comm=podman-init cmdline=/run/podman-init -- /usr/bin/ceph-osd -n osd.2 -f --setuser ceph --setgroup ceph --default-log-to-file=false --default-log-to-journald=true --default-log-to-stderr=false --osd-objectstore=bluestore
  1301 1229 0:43 / /rootfs/home/ubuntu/cephtest/mnt.0 rw,nosuid,nodev,relatime - fuse.ceph-fuse ceph-fuse rw,user_id=0,group_id=0,allow_other

With that hint, a tiny LLM query pointed to check rslave vs. rprivate flags for kernel mount propogation types and that led me to check the cephadm source and finally the aha moment.

Use rslave (as ceph-volume already does) so host (u)mounts propagate into the containers.

Assisted-by: Gemini
Fixes: http://tracker.ceph.com/issues/64502

72968.title: test/osd: Fix flaky pg vulnerability duration unit test
72968.author: sseshasa
72968.body:
The test `VulnerabilityWindowNewReplicaInheritsOpenWindow` was failing 2 out of 1000 attempts with:

Expected: (sum_ns) > (0u), actual: 0 vs 0.

This is due to the vulnerability window lasting for sub 1 msec time in the rare case resulting in the window getting discarded as expected. Sub millisecond windows are discarded as it keeps `pg_vulnerability_duration_min` meaningful for the actual use case. Letting sub-millisecond noise would make the "smallest real exposure window" signal less useful.

Fix the test by introducing a 10 msec sleep just after the window opens so that it's open past the 1 msec duration. The same 10 msec sleep exists for all other tests, but was missed for this test.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81922
Signed-off-by: Sridhar Seshasayee <sridhar.seshasayee@ibm.com>

72969.title: mgr/dashboard: preserve CRUSH tree expanded state on refresh
72969.author: vobruba-martin
72969.body:
The CRUSH map viewer polls the cluster every 5 seconds and rebuilds the whole tree with every node hard-coded to `expanded: true`. The state of nodes the user collapsed was only held inside Carbon's TreeNodeComponent, so each background refresh expanded them again, making large CRUSH maps very hard to navigate.

Track the IDs of collapsed nodes in the component via the `nodetoggle` event and use them when rebuilding the tree. New nodes still default to expanded.

Also track tree nodes by their CRUSH id instead of object identity, so Angular reuses the existing DOM nodes instead of re-rendering the whole tree on every poll (which also kept resetting the selected node).

72973.title: crimson/net: defer msgr2 acks, bounded by time and size
72973.author: ronen-fr
72973.body:
On lossless (OSD-OSD) connections, crimson writes a standalone ack frame for
almost every received message, even though every outgoing message already
carries the ack in its header (`ack_seq`). On replicated writes, close to half
of the socket writes carry only an ack.

This PR is based on, and includes until they merge:
- fad2b6d584 "crimson/net: don't write an ack frame for every received message"
  from #72685 (Matan): acks ride on outgoing messages, and an ack frame is
  written only once 64 messages are unacked.
- The messenger metrics from #72580 (de0d3ca9defd, 5d0cff184e17).

On top of these, it adds:
- **Bounds on deferred acks.** An ack frame becomes due when no message carried
  the ack within `crimson_msgr_ack_delay` (5ms), or when
  `crimson_msgr_ack_max_pending_msgs` (64) messages or
  `crimson_msgr_ack_max_pending_bytes` (4MiB) of payload are unacked. Without
  the time bound, once traffic stops the peer keeps up to 63 delivered
  messages, for as long as the connection stays idle.
  `crimson_msgr_ack_delay=0` restores the ack-per-message behavior.
- **Acks owed across a reconnect.** An ack still owed when the connection
  reopens (after a fault, possibly on another reactor) is written right away.
- **Counters.** `msgr_ack_frames_sent`, `msgr_ack_frames_received`,
  `msgr_acks_forced_by_timer`, `msgr_acks_forced_by_limit`.
- **Tests.** `test_v2_lossless_connected_fault2` injects faults on ack frames,
  so it now runs with a delay of 0. A new test, `test_v2_lossless_deferred_ack`,
  checks that an outgoing message carries the ack and that the message limit
  forces an ack frame.
- **perf_crimson_msgr.** The tool used only lossy connections, which never
  ack. It now has:
  - `--msgr-policy lossless`, for OSD-OSD-like connections;
  - `--server-reply-delay-us`, to model a replica's commit latency;
  - `--ceph-option name=value`, to set config options;
  - a report of each side's messenger counters.

Early results: perf_crimson_msgr, lossless, 1 connection, depth 64, 4K
messages, loopback, single runs:

| server reply delay | ack delay 0 (old behavior)          | default (5ms / 64)        |
|--------------------|-------------------------------------|---------------------------|
| 0                  | 63.8K IOPS, ~50% of writes ack-only | 81.2K IOPS, 0 ack frames  |
| 500us              | 57.8K IOPS, ~51% ack-only           | 67.5K IOPS, 8 ack frames  |

These measure the messenger alone. Cluster numbers (3 OSDs, CyanStore, ack
delay 0 vs. default) will follow.

Related-to: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80545

72974.title: mgr/dashboard: allow the user to edit non default rgw entities
72974.author: aaSharma14
72974.body:
**Description**

This PR fixes RGW multisite management for non-default realms, zonegroups, zones, and storage classes.

**Root cause**

1. radosgw-admin finds zones and zonegroups by name across the whole cluster, but it only uses the realm for period commits.
2. With no zonegroup given, it falls back to the default zonegroup.
3. So many dashboard operations quietly hit the default entities or failed for non-default ones.

**Backend**

1. Realm and zonegroup passed through: every radosgw-admin call for zones, zonegroups and placement targets now carries the realm and zonegroup. This covers zone delete, add and remove zone, listing and deleting placement targets, and looking up placement by ID.
2. Realm lookup: there is a new lookup of the realm from a zonegroup, and the existing zone-to-realm lookup now logs errors instead of swallowing them.
3. Storage classes in non-default zonegroups: adding, editing or placing a storage class on a zone now names the zonegroup. This fixes the error "storage class 'X' is not defined in zonegroup 'default-placement' placement target".
4. Storage-class API errors: the storage-class POST and PUT calls raised a TypeError because the realm name was required, and that is fixed.

**Frontend**

1. Edit forms: the realm, zonegroup and zone forms now handle non-default entities and drop the default-only restrictions.
2. Storage-class screens: the service and list pass the zonegroup on delete and when loading placement targets.
3. Delete notification: the notification used to read "Removed Storage Class 'undefined'", and it now shows the real name.
4. Two-click submit: the create form needed two clicks because the hidden target_endpoint field was always required. It is now required only for cloud and glacier types.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82018

72975.title: crimson: send replication from each reactor's cluster lane
72975.author: knrt10
72975.body:
Every `send_to_osd()` went through the one cluster messenger on reactor 0, so repops and repop replies were all sent from there.

Each reactor now has its own cluster. `messenger. send_to_osd()` uses that lane, so the send happens on the reactor that generated the message. The published cluster messenger is unchanged: peers still dial the osdmap address, and incoming ops are dispatched as before. A lane listens on its own port and is used for the connections it opened. No osdmap or placement change.

Lane handshakes still authenticate through the MonClient on reactor 0. The auth steps run there and copy the session key back. That hop is only during the handshake.

A repop reply is sent on the connection the repop arrived on, as Classic does. The primary reads that reply on its lane. 

On the replica, the reply is still a cross-core send when the socket's reactor is not the PG's.
When a peer goes down, mark_down_all_ports() closes every session with that peer's type, IP, and nonce, on any port, so its lanes are marked down too.


Part of: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80545
